The combination unites two classic species of founder: Laberge dropped out of high school to pursue his first company, which did similar fluid analysis for large construction machines that depend on hydraulics. Adams was an academic, trained as a physicist, who spent much of his career developing advanced ocean sensing technology as an MIT professor and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute researcher before starting his company. Now, with Adams as the company’s chief science officer, the combined teams are working to integrate both technologies into one sensor, which they expect to have on the market by early next year. Omen’s initial sensors will be monitoring chips pulling in 250 to 300 MW of power by the end of the year, worth about $5 to $7 billion, Laberge told TechCrunch, with the hope of being installed on the equivalent of 1 GW of chips by the end of 2027. The added value is in uptime: If the fluid system gets out of whack, data center operators typically choose to dump the water rather than risk damage to their expensive equipment. That means shutting down operations until the fluid system is restored, which costs a lot of money. Monitoring lets data center operators use the same fluid for longer, and minimize the costs of a clean up. Adams hopes to see their technologies have an impact outside of data centers as well, telling TechCrunch that “water goes into data centers, and then it comes out and gets dumped into municipal water, and you want that whole process to happen in a way that’s as safe and responsible as possible — and that means you got to measure stuff.” AI companies once estimated as much as $4 trillion would be spent on AI infrastructure by 2030, but some investors have grown skeptical of the buildout , sending hyperscaler stocks plummeting in recent days. Omen’s team isn’t worried about shifting sentiment though, since their work comes after a data center has been built. “We’re working customers on stuff they’re building today or have already built, and so it doesn’t really affect us because all of those projects were financed 12 months ago,” Laberge said. “Our view is, if there’s tightness, this is still going to be the biggest market in human history, even if you sliced it in half.”

title: OpenAI is finally merging ChatGPT’s Chat and Work tabs
abstract: The ChatGPT desktop app can be a confusing piece of software, given that there are ChatGPT and Codex sections, and within the former, there are Chat and Work tabs. With so many options, it’s sometimes easy to forget where you are working and where exactly your project is. In an apparent effort to address this, OpenAI is now gearing up to merge the Chat and Work tabs within the ChatGPT experience, according to an email sent to users. OpenAI said that initially, this experience will be available to select users for feedback before it is rolled out widely. “This will enable you to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place. You can bring in your files and plugins and ask ChatGPT to build a website, create a presentation, or do things for you on the web, while reviewing and guiding its work. Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app,” the email said. OpenAI also said with this transition, both ChatGPT and Codex will draw tokens from the same allowance pool. It said this change won’t impact most users, but based on usage and model, some folks might need to wait for resets more frequently. Rival Anthropic merged Claude’s chat and Cowork functions into one screen in September.

title: OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’
abstract: Data centers are deeply unpopular . But what if we called them something else? Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too . The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “ the issue” in the presidential election. So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI “speed limits” ; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards; and yes — rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.” Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments ) as “good and healthy.” “Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said.

title: Data centers are now a midterm issue, even in Brooklyn
abstract: On Thursday evening, I slipped on my neon yellow heels and a floral mini dress. It’s New York, so I can wear whatever I want to a midterm election event full of media types, techies, policy advocates, and, well, does anyone else even exist at these things? I walked into the dimly blue-lit Brooklyn warehouse and was surprised to see the room already filling up. Newsreel, the media company founded by former Forbes and Newsweek reporter Jack Brewster, hosted the event, and the lineup was heavy-hitting. Kenneth Schlenker, co-founder of the focus app Opal, sat down for a fireside chat about “the state of attention,” and Aryan Ranjan, who built the campaign management software Baraza, gave a midterm forecast. I, meanwhile, was moderating a panel on data centers. Brewster said the goal was for people to “put their phones away and talk to each other about the election, five days out.” As the evening progressed, however, one topic consumed nearly every conversation: AI, data centers, and the backlash against the growing technocracy. Lately, as a tech reporter, I’ve noticed a growing chasm between tech and everyone else. I spend most of my days talking to people who see the benefits of AI, who are so ambitious in building it and so optimistic that it will succeed that, when I talk to people beyond the tech world, I forget how ugly it all seems to them. Outside the tech bubble, data centers and AI have become such an intense ballot-box issue that they could sway some midterm races on November 3. Newsreel’s Midterm Madness Image Credits: Taylor Williams / Newsreel A recent report from Data Center Watch found that almost $200 billion in data center projects were delayed, stalled, or blocked in the first half of 2026 due to political and community opposition. Meanwhile, states like Pennsylvania, Georgia, Texas, New York, and Virginia are considering more guardrails and transparency around data centers’ rapid development. Hundreds of new data centers are planned in Virginia alone, a state already nicknamed the “data center capital of the world.” A fireside chat with New York City Council member Chi Ossé, just before my panel, set the tone. AI came up near the end; Ossé said he doesn’t really use it. To me, though, he didn’t seem to be for or against it. He mostly emphasized that he would like to see tech executives held more accountable and trillionaires like Elon Musk taxed more. He described himself as a democratic socialist, but a “law and order” one. When CEOs talk about a technology that could deplete 10% of human civilization, he said, “they should be called to testify in front of Congress.” My panel was up next. I moderated a discussion with Maia Woluchem, a technology and human rights researcher, and Hilary Flint, an environmental and public health advocate, about data centers. As I took the stage, I decided to get a better read on the crowd. I asked, “Who here is pro-AI data center?” and was promptly booed. Our conversation covered a range of topics and emotions. People are upset that big tech companies appear to be cutting secret deals with local officials to build billion-dollar data centers. In some cases, zoning rules make it unclear what is being built until it’s too late to protest. Newsreel’s Midterm Madness Image Credits: Taylor Williams / Newsreel At the same time, people are struggling with the cost of living and doing everything they can to hold onto what’s left of the American Dream, while tech leaders talk about AI replacing workers, or even humanity itself. Residents feel they have lost control over what happens in their communities, and they worry about the environmental and health risks. The panel agreed that data centers are the physical embodiment of people’s fears and anger toward the tech class and the rapid pace of technology. “What is a life worth?” Flint said when I brought up the benefits that some communities have seen from data center build-outs. People still protest, she said, because they “value their lives a little bit more than a temporary check.” The panel after mine featured NewsNation host Batya Ungar-Sargon; political strategist Morris Katz, who worked on Zohran Mamdani’s campaign; and Vox’s Astead Herndon. They were supposed to be talking about the future of the Democratic Party. But once again, the conversation shifted to data centers. Ungar-Sargon noted that some labor unions support data centers because of the jobs they promise. (Reports show that data centers create many jobs initially, but those jobs are not permanent once construction ends.) “There used to be a lot of pride in a community in the Rust Belt about very ugly, enormous buildings in their communities because everybody worked there,” she said, nodding to an earlier comment I’d made about data centers being ugly. “And they knew that building represented prosperity for themselves, stability for their children, and a future and a piece of the American dream.” Newsreel’s Midterm Madness Image Credits: Taylor Williams / Newsreel Herndon noted that Vivek Ramaswamy was booed for making a similar point in Ohio, a Rust Belt state. “I just want to reinforce the lack of consent happening,” he said. “Because that’s true among Republicans in those places and I’ve watched it.” Katz was also skeptical. “It’s the same people who have taken so many union jobs away,” he said. “The same institutional powers that have robbed labor and working people of jobs and profit. Now coming back to essentially finish the job and take whatever scraps remain.” Along the warehouse walls, I noticed sticky notes answering posted questions, including “Will we ever be able to get Big Money out of politics?” “God, I hope so,” one note said. People rushed the bar when the panel ended, and techno music began to blast. They broke into small groups, where AI and data centers were once again the topic, this time in more private conversations. I asked Brewster if he was surprised by how much of the conversation focused on AI and data centers. “It came up in every conversation onstage, and it was the second-most common topic in the questions people sent us when they RSVP’d,” he said, adding that it was happening even in New York, where data centers aren’t very visible. “AI has become an election issue for regular voters,” he said. “In rural communities, the backlash is about feeling replaced. In a place like Brooklyn, it’s more about who gets rich from it.” Before leaving, I made the rounds, asking people to name the craziest thing they’d seen in tech this year. Two tech founders mentioned the AI assistant startup Instinct, while a non-tech person named Sam Altman Another non-tech person brought up the rise of deepfakes and AI art. AI art, she said, is starting to signal cheapness. That may be why luxury brands are going the other way: Prada’s holiday campaign features hand-drawn illustrations , and Hermès has been spotlighting artists’ handmade work on Instagram. Newsreel’s Midterm Madness Image Credits: Taylor Williams / Newsreel On my way out, I spoke to a software engineer who said the craziest thing she’d seen this year was a person who painted their nails orange for Halloween and was asked if it was a tribute to the Anthropic IPO. I admitted that I, too, had once worn a burnt orange dress and briefly thought of myself as the Claude logo. She later told me data centers are popping up in her Southern California hometown, too. Hearing that, I thought for the first time about how I’d feel if one popped up in mine. She grew up in a Chinese immigrant community, where neighbors are putting signs in their yards showing dragons choking a data center. The signs have since been translated into other languages, she said.

title: Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones
abstract: AI Entertainment Gaming Anthropic clamps down on Claude’s AI video game clones Anthropic is steering Claude away from re-creating specific titles, but users can still use it to make their own games. Anthropic is steering Claude away from re-creating specific titles, but users can still use it to make their own games. by Jay Peters Nov 2, 2026, 6:56 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Part Of Reverse-engineered games: All the news on video game decomps, recomps, VR and web and 3D ports see all updates Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme. Anthropic has updated Claude Code’s system prompt to prevent the AI tool from being used to re-create existing video games, as reported by Tom’s Hardware . Retro gaming is currently being overrun with AI-made decompilations, recompilations, and ports , but while Anthropic will still let people use Claude Code to make games, it doesn’t want people to use it for direct clones. Last week, a user on X posted a screenshot allegedly showing two new sentences added to Claude Code’s system prompt: “Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is named or called original.” Anthropic’s Addy Osmani, in a reply , didn’t confirm that specific language but did say that the company had updated the prompt in Claude Code on Opus 5.5: We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy. Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that’s yours, send it my way. We’ve asked Anthropic if it has or will be updating other Claude system prompts as well. title: OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas
abstract: AI News Science OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas As public opinion has soured on data centers, it’s selling ‘AI campuses’ as protectors, instead of noisy polluters. As public opinion has soured on data centers, it’s selling ‘AI campuses’ as protectors, instead of noisy polluters. by Emma Roth Nov 2, 2026, 6:01 PM UTC Image: The Verge Part Of All the latest updates on AI data centers see all updates Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO. In an announcement on Monday , OpenAI says it will pilot its “Grid Protectors Program” at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes. The announcement comes as opposition to data centers spreads across the US, in response to massive projects that have begun development and construction, frequently with little or no input from local residents. In Utah, residents protested after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double the state’s peak electricity demand in 2025, and spread hot air in the desert valley surrounding the data center. Now OpenAI’s approach is to pitch the construction of power plants that feed the electricity required by the new AI data centers it’s building as “a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.” Several states like Tennessee, Florida, Oklahoma, Oregon, and others have enacted laws that say they will prevent AI companies from passing energy costs on to residents, in addition to moratoriums and other restrictions. This is besides the environmental impacts, as a recent study by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) said that powering proposed Texas data center projects could undo decades of air quality gains over just five years. OpenAI, which has switched to calling its AI data centers “compute campuses” in an effort to separate from their poor public reputation , claims it helps reduce costs for customers by operating year-round: “Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times,” OpenAI’s announcement says. “Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest.” OpenAI says it’s going to continue working with policymakers and utility services to make “arrangements for our future campus to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.” Along with its data center in Georgia, OpenAI is also partnering with Oracle and SoftBank to build its “Stargate” data centers across the US, including in Shackelford County, Texas; Doña Ana County, New Mexico; and Milam County, Texas. title: The New York Times sues Brave web browser for AI scraping and bypassing paywalls
abstract: Tech AI News The New York Times sues Brave web browser for AI scraping and bypassing paywalls Brave has allegedly provided ‘stolen copyrighted content’ to many AI companies.﻿ Brave has allegedly provided ‘stolen copyrighted content’ to many AI companies.﻿ by Jay Peters Nov 2, 2026, 5:51 PM UTC Photo: NurPhoto via Getty Images Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme. The New York Times and a group of other publications have filed lawsuits against the company that makes the Brave web browser over alleged unlawful scraping to train AI and also letting users bypass their paywalls, as reported by Reuters . According to a complaint filed by the New York Daily News , the Chicago Tribune , and the Orlando Sentinel , Brave Software has monetized its index of scraped websites by, in part, providing AI companies with paid access to “real-time online content from the Brave Index.” The AI companies then use that index to train their models, access content to “respond to specific user queries,” or both. Brave has allegedly provided “stolen copyrighted content” to “many” AI companies including Anthropic, Perplexity, Mistral, xAI, and Cohere. Brave also promotes “hundreds of top publishers” as being accessible through its “Paywall blocker” feature in its browser. “Brave has never asked for the Publishers’ permission to access their websites, much less to copy the material and provide it to users or other AI companies,” the complaint says. “On the contrary, as noted above, Brave allows its users to bypass the Publishers’ paywalls without their consent, and has taken other steps that prevent the Publishers from blocking Brave’s access to the Publishers’ websites. Brave has never compensated the Publishers for the unlawful use, copying, and distribution of the Publishers’ copyrighted content.” “While we believe in the ethical and responsible use and development of AI, Brave has flouted established copyright law and ignored repeated requests by The Times to stop its infringing conduct,” Graham James, an NYT spokesperson, says in a statement to The Verge . “We filed this lawsuit to hold Brave accountable for stealing our content to power its own products and to provide it to some of the most prominent and well resourced generative AI companies in the world.” “AI giants are now desperate to avoid getting caught red-handed stealing news from publishers, so Brave Software is selling them a back door to the journalism they know they have no right to,” says Steven Lieberman, the attorney who filed the lawsuit on behalf of the other three publications. “Buying stolen goods secondhand doesn’t make them legitimate. Brave must be held responsible for laundering pirated reporting for the AI industry.” Brave, Anthropic, Mistral, SpaceXSI, and Cohere didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. “ The New York Times is overpaying its attorneys and underpaying its journalists. (Who could’ve easily identified the disinformation in this suit.)” says Jesse Dwyer, Perplexity’s chief communications officer. Update, November 2nd : Clarified that one lawsuit was filed by New York Daily News , the Chicago Tribune , and the Orlando Sentinel , not the companies that run them. Also added a statement from the attorney who filed the lawsuit on behalf of those publications. title: Deep Principle Releases Hydrogen-1.0: A 753B Open-Weight Model for Scientific Discovery
abstract: Deep Principle has released Hydrogen-1.0 , an open-weight scientific model for chemistry, materials science and life sciences. It is built by post-training Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 on domain data, laboratory records and agent discovery trajectories. For developers, it offers open weights that report a FrontierScience-Research win over GPT-6-Astra. The weights ship under the MIT License. Hydrogen-1.0 is a scientific research assistant model from Deep Principle, a Hangzhou-based AI-for-materials company. The model card describes it as a GLM-5.3 derivative for scientific problem solving. It targets question framing, experiment planning, results analysis and open-ended discovery. Deep Principle team states that proprietary models produced recent AI science results, but their discovery capabilities are not open. Hydrogen-1.0 is its attempt at a reproducible, inspectable alternative. The pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). Data comes from 4 sources: Infrastructure builds on Megatron and SGLang across NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm. The team keeps dynamic sparse attention causal across context-parallel shards. Muon optimizer state is moved between CPU, GPU and disk per backend. RL uses resumable rollouts, and each token keeps its original behavior log-probability for importance correction. A layout adapter converts training checkpoints into BF16 and 128×128 blockwise FP8 inference weights. Full datasets and recipes are not released. On public benchmarks, Deep Principle reports Hydrogen-1.0 outperforms GPT-6-Astra on FrontierScience-Research. The tweet thread from one of the founders’ report 93.0% on GPQA-Diamond. That improves on GLM-5.3 and roughly matches Kimi-K3, per the blog. Internal research-task evals compare it with GPT-6-Astra at maximum thinking: In transition metal complex design, models chased a larger HOMO-LUMO gap over 5 rounds. By round 5, Hydrogen-1.0 reached a mean best-so-far gap of 4.318 eV. GPT-6-Astra reached 3.689 eV and Kimi-K3 reached 3.353 eV. On 117 experiment-planning questions, Hydrogen-1.0 scored above Kimi-K3. GPT-6-Astra and Opus-5.5 were excluded after refusing more than 50% of requests. The technical post shows 4 demos . Hydrogen-1.0 writes Python to build a polyethylene melt and runs GROMACS. It detects a topology error, repairs it, and analyzes the corrected 40 ns trajectory. It grows an Ireland-Claisen reaction network of 27 structures through 30 plausible reactions. It ranks 7 candidate monoformylation products of 2-bromonaphthalene from a 1H NMR trace. It also writes a JSON protocol for a 12-vial Suzuki coupling study. A virtual lab compilation step catches an aspiration without a fresh tip before execution. Weights are on Hugging Face and ModelScope . Deep Principle team tested BF16 serving with SGLang on 8 GPUs using tensor parallelism of 8. NVFP4 targets NVIDIA B200 and B300. MXFP4 targets AMD Instinct MI350X and MI355X. The server exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with a reasoning_effort setting. title: NVIDIA Releases Auto Ontology: An Open Semantic Layer That Grounds AI Agent SQL
abstract: NVIDIA has released Auto Ontology , an open library under the Apache 2.0 license . NVIDIA Auto Ontology is a semantic layer framework that builds a context layer from enterprise metadata. Agents use that layer to write SQL against certified business definitions. The repository states the problem plainly: a fast revenue answer is worthless if the number is wrong. It is a context layer that sits between an agent and the data warehouse. It tells the agent where data lives and what fields mean. It also says whether to use a field, how to use it, and where it came from. NVIDIA’s developer page frames the output as a starting ontology. Business experts still test, refine and certify it. The stack has 4 core services. A Next.js 16 frontend handles the web UI and authentication on port 3000. A FastAPI backend with LangChain runs chat, NL-to-SQL and catalog APIs on port 3001. An ingestion worker writes embeddings on port 3002. Postgres with pgvector stores the catalog, the ontology and the vectors. Source databases can be Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake or DuckDB. Models are set through environment “triplets” of endpoint, key and model. Separate roles exist for reasoning, non-reasoning, embedding and reranking. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works. The MCP server docs describe 9 read-only tools. ask_question returns the answer, the SQL and the rows as separate fields. Results cap at 100 rows. check_readiness confirms a compiled semantic layer and a live database connection exist. There is no tool for browsing raw schemas. NVIDIA chose that on purpose, so agents reach data through the semantic layer. The underlying OpenAPI spec publishes 87 operations. Sign-in runs through OAuth, and every call carries the signed-in user’s permissions. NVIDIA ships a separate harness, auto-ontology-eval . It runs 2 arms in NeMo Gym: a schema-only LLM control and the ontology-grounded agent. Scoring is deterministic execution match, with no LLM judge. Bundled datasets include BIRD Dev (1,534 questions, 11 databases) and Mini-Dev (500 questions). FDABench-Lite adds 169 questions, and BEAVER defaults to a 100-question sample. The harness repo adds 2 limitations. Optional few-shot exemplars and value anchors go to the ontology arm only. A delta measured with them covers those inputs, not grounding alone. Its tested configuration also routes both arms through a Claude model on NVIDIA’s inference gateway. Local setup is docker compose up -d --build after filling in .env . Kubernetes users get a Helm chart and a DEPLOYMENT.md guide. NVIDIA team also publishes the backend as an NGC container . An NVIDIA API key from build.nvidia.com covers the default models. Check out the GitHub repo , the eval harness and the MCP docs . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . title: Meet qwenGPU: Qwen3.5-2B With 45 Compiled GPU Layers That Run CUDA
abstract: qwenGPU is an experimental model that compiles a SIMT GPU directly into the weights of Qwen3.5-2B . Developer Vixhal ( @TheVixhal ) released it on GitHub under the MIT license. The model runs real CUDA, compiled to NVIDIA PTX, inside its own forward passes. For developers, it tests one idea: exact computation inside a pretrained LLM, not beside it. qwenGPU is Qwen3.5-2B with 45 compiled transformer layers placed in front of Qwen’s own 24. None of those layers are trained. A compiler computes every weight. The GPU is a 4-lane SIMT machine. It has 15 registers per lane, a 4-stage pipeline, a 32-block ROM and 126 memory words. It uses only Qwen3.5’s own layer types: Gated DeltaNet linear attention and SwiGLU MLPs. The trick is the Gated DeltaNet recurrent state. In the circuit’s heads, the gate is held open and the write strength is 1. Every key is one-hot. Each update overwrites exactly 1 row, and a one-hot query reads it back. So each row works as a memory cell. That state holds the program ROM, registers and global memory. The README lists 16 register rows per lane, with 1 that always reads zero. That matches the 15 usable registers in the X post. The GPU supports integer arithmetic, predicates, divergent branches and loops. It also supports shared memory, atomicAdd , __syncthreads() and warp shuffles. The host plays the role of NVRTC and the CUDA driver. It compiles CUDA to PTX with clang, then lowers PTX to machine blocks. It feeds the program and input arrays to the model as tokens. From there, the model writes the launch itself. Each EXEC(b, w) token runs block b for warp w in 1 forward pass. The VAL tokens after it carry register results. Memory writes return as MEM records. The host reads results from the recurrent state and computes none of them. In the demo video , a dot product of [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6] returns 32. The model wrote that launch in 47 tokens. Meet qwenGPU: Qwen3.5-2B with a SIMT GPU inside its weights, 45 compiled layers in front of Qwen’s own, using its Gated DeltaNet layers as registers and memory. It runs real CUDA in its forward passes. The host compiles the kernel to PTX and loads it, then the model writes every… pic.twitter.com/iM5IETEbIv Not by the developer’s measure. The circuit is muted on text tokens, and Qwen’s own weights are unchanged. The merged model’s next-token distribution stays within a KL of about 7e-4 of the original. All numbers are self-reported, measured on Apple silicon with MPS in bf16: In normal mode, Qwen writes an expression like [1, 2, 3] @ [4, 5, 6] for ready-made kernels. In advanced mode, Qwen writes the CUDA kernel itself. The README warns that a 2B model’s CUDA is still unreliable. qwenGPU uses the transformer compiler from Qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal. Qwenputer compiles a 32-bit RISC-V CPU into Qwen3.5-4B. Percepta built a WebAssembly interpreter into a transformer with 2D attention heads in March 2026. The speed figures use different hardware and token types, so they are not directly comparable. The quickstart needs Python 3.11+, uv, just and about 16 GB of free memory. Advanced mode also needs clang with the NVPTX backend. just build downloads Qwen3.5-2B and compiles the GPU into it. No prebuilt checkpoint is published. A built checkpoint falls under Qwen’s Apache-2.0 license. Check out the GitHub repo , the qgpu CUDA reference , the Qwen3.5-2B model card and the original X post . title: Running LLMs Locally Does Not Mean Your Data Is Safe: What Cohere’s Study Reveals
abstract: Running LLMs Locally Does Not Mean Your Data Is Safe: What Cohere’s Study Reveals Cohere caught Alibaba’s Qwen model unexpectedly attempting to upload a test payload to Alibaba Cloud storage during a cybersecurity task, but the sandbox blocked the request, leaving questions about what triggered the behavior. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on November 2, 2026 in Language Models Running a large language model (LLM) locally is often considered the safest option for developers who want more control over their data. You download the model weights, run everything on your own hardware, and avoid sending sensitive information to external AI providers. But does that automatically make your AI system secure? A recent investigation by Cohere has raised some interesting questions. During a security benchmark, researchers observed an open-weight Qwen model attempting to send data to an Alibaba Cloud server, despite receiving no instructions to do so. The findings quickly sparked a debate about model security, training data, and whether running LLMs locally really protects users. I think there is more to this story than blaming a single model. Let us look at what actually happened, what the community thinks, and why the entire AI agent setup matters. What Did Cohere Find? On October 26, 2026, Cohere published an investigation into unusual behavior from Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next , an open-weight language model. The researchers were evaluating the model using Microsoft's CTI-REALM cybersecurity benchmark. The assigned task was straightforward: write a detection rule to identify suspicious commands that download and execute malicious shell scripts. Instead, the model unexpectedly started exploring its environment. According to Cohere, it inspected temporary files, checked available command-line utilities, examined DNS configuration, and attempted to upload a test payload to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket located in Beijing. What made this particularly interesting was that the model's visible reasoning indicated that it would not execute any tools. Fortunately, the researchers were using an isolated sandbox without outbound network access, so the upload attempt failed. The payload was also a fixed test string, not demonstrated private user data. Cohere reported that this behavior occurred in fewer than one in 100,000 evaluation calls . Repeating the same original prompt produced a normal detection rule. The investigation therefore demonstrates a rare and unexpected tool action. It does not prove that Alibaba deliberately introduced a backdoor or that sensitive information was successfully leaked. What Does the AI Community Think? Cohere's investigation sparked heated discussions across Reddit's LocalLLaMA community and LinkedIn , with developers questioning both the findings and the reproduction methodology. One major criticism focused on prefilling . Cohere's released script supplies 2,323 tokens of previously recorded reasoning and commands, stopping just before URL generation. Critics argued that this setup effectively encourages the model to complete a suspicious command rather than demonstrating that it would independently initiate one. However, Cohere clarified on Reddit that the original incident occurred without prefilling. The technique was introduced afterward to investigate the behavior, which reportedly occurred in fewer than one in 100,000 evaluation calls. Other developers suggested that the Alibaba URLs might be training artifacts rather than evidence of malicious intent . Models exposed to agent logs, cloud storage commands, and similar examples during training could reproduce those patterns in unrelated tasks. Some community members also questioned whether proprietary models would exhibit similar behavior under identical tests. earlier community reports had already described unexpected Alibaba Cloud URLs appearing during normal Qwen usage, suggesting the phenomenon was not limited to Cohere's experiments. The debate also highlighted a broader concern: running an open-weight model locally does not automatically make an AI agent secure . Models with terminal access and unrestricted network permissions can still attempt unexpected operations, making sandboxing and network restrictions essential. Ultimately, the investigation raises legitimate questions about AI agent security, but the available evidence does not establish an intentional backdoor. Reproducing suspicious behavior and proving malicious intent are two very different things. Why Training Data Might Explain This Behavior One thing I find particularly interesting about this incident is how training data can influence an AI model's behavior, sometimes in unexpected ways. LLMs learn patterns from enormous amounts of text, code, conversations, and tool-use examples. If a model encounters thousands of examples involving particular cloud services, shell commands, or debugging workflows, it may reproduce similar patterns later. For example, a coding agent might associate debugging with downloading files or making network requests, even when those actions are unnecessary for the current task. This could explain why Qwen generated Alibaba Cloud URLs. The model may have learned those patterns from its training data rather than deliberately attempting to send information elsewhere. There is also the possibility of training-data poisoning , where malicious examples are introduced into training or fine-tuning data to influence future model behavior. However, these explanations remain speculative. We don't have enough evidence to determine what caused the behavior observed by Cohere. And that brings me to what I think is the more important issue: what happens when a model's unexpected output is allowed to execute? The Bigger Security Problem Is the Agent Harness A language model cannot independently access your files or send data over the internet. It needs tools and an execution environment that allow it to perform those actions. This is where the agent harness becomes important. The harness is the software surrounding the model. It manages context, tool execution, permissions, filesystem access, and interactions with external services. Think about coding agents such as Claude Code , Codex CLI , or other local agent systems. The model decides what action to propose, but the harness controls how that action is executed. If an agent has unrestricted terminal access, permission to read sensitive files, and outbound network access, an unexpected command can become a serious security problem. The same model running in an isolated environment might generate the identical command without being able to execute it successfully. There is research supporting this distinction. In the recent HarnessSecurity-Bench study, researchers evaluated security mechanisms across six coding-agent harnesses, including Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Qwen Code . Under their controlled testing conditions, enabling automatic tool approval increased attack success from 29.2% to 95.6% . That is a substantial difference caused by the security configuration of the agent system rather than a change to the underlying model. The researchers also found that network isolation and read-only execution reduced successful attacks, although these restrictions could make legitimate tasks harder to complete. This is why I think the discussion should go beyond whether Qwen intentionally generated a suspicious URL. How Can We Make Local AI Agents Safer? I don't think the solution is to stop using open-weight models. Instead, we need to be more careful about what our AI agents are allowed to do. Security experts at OWASP recommend sandboxing, restricting tool permissions, and limiting network access when deploying coding agents. Here are a few practical steps you can take: Run agents in a sandbox: Use Docker containers, virtual machines, or tools like Anthropic's Sandbox Runtime to isolate command execution.

title: 5 AI Certifications Worth Paying For in 2026 (And Which to Skip)
abstract: 5 AI Certifications Worth Paying For in 2026 (And Which to Skip) A data-backed guide to the credentials that actually move the needle for data scientists and machine learning practitioners. By Vinod Chugani on November 2, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence The AI certification market has exploded. By 2026, AI credentials account for nearly 30% of all professional certifications being pursued, a 20x increase from pre-ChatGPT levels, according to labor market research from Revelio Labs . That growth has produced two very different categories: a handful of credentials that employers actively screen for and that correlate with measurable salary premiums, and a large pile of programs that generate revenue for their creators while delivering almost no hiring signal to the people who buy them. Here's the uncomfortable reality: most AI certifications aren't worth it. The candidates who get hired tend to have fewer certifications and more production experience. Five certifications with no portfolio is a red flag to senior hiring managers. One strong cloud certification paired with a GitHub repository of deployed projects is far more convincing. That said, some credentials do matter, for specific, concrete reasons. The credentialing organization already has employer trust. The exam tests production-relevant skills rather than rote recall. The credential actually shows up in job postings. This guide covers five that check all three boxes, along with an honest look at what to skip and why. Two things are worth flagging before the list. First, the AWS Certified Machine Learning Specialty (MLS-C01) was permanently retired on March 31, 2026. You'll still find it recommended across the web on pages that were never updated, but it can no longer be taken. Second, Microsoft's AI-102 certification (Azure AI Engineer Associate) is being updated as of late 2026. Check Microsoft's official certification page for current status before scheduling that exam. The 5 AI Certifications Worth Paying For 1. Google Cloud Professional Machine Learning Engineer Cost: \$200 | Level: Professional | Exam duration: 2 hours | Renewal: Every 2 years Who it's for: Experienced machine learning engineers and data scientists who build and deploy production machine learning systems, particularly those working in or targeting Google Cloud environments. This is the highest-impact cloud machine learning certification available in 2026. Multiple salary analyses report that holders see roughly a 25% salary premium compared to peers without it. That's the largest differential of any machine learning certification in current data. The exam covers the full machine learning engineering lifecycle on Google Cloud: designing and building pipelines with Vertex AI , productionizing and monitoring models at scale, and selecting appropriate machine learning approaches for specific business constraints. A significant June 2026 update added generative AI content, including building solutions using Vertex AI Agent Builder and Model Garden . That makes this exam substantially broader than it was two years ago and considerably more relevant to where the hiring market actually is right now. Google recommends at least three years of industry experience and one year on Google Cloud before sitting the exam. This isn't a credential to chase right after finishing your first machine learning course. The pass rate is estimated as moderate, and hands-on experience matters far more than memorized definitions. Why it's worth it: Employer recognition is strong. The credential shows up in a meaningful share of machine learning engineering job postings, and the June 2026 update aligns the content with current production AI work rather than classical machine learning alone. It also opens paths to related Google credentials, including the newer Cloud GenAI Engineer certification (\$200) for those who want to go deeper on generative AI application development. Best pairing: The Google Cloud Skills Boost GenAI learning path (free, self-paced) before the exam. Google Cloud Professional Machine Learning Engineer: Registration and Exam Details 2. AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer – Associate (MLA-C01) Cost: \$150 | Level: Associate | Exam duration: 130 minutes, 65 questions | Important note: MLA-C01 is the current AWS machine learning credential (MLA-C02 is in beta as of 2026) Who it's for: Machine learning engineers, data engineers, and applied scientists building production machine learning systems on AWS. When AWS retired the Machine Learning Specialty (MLS-C01) in March 2026, it replaced it with the AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer – Associate (MLA-C01). The old Specialty exam was deep but narrow, leaning heavily on classical machine learning algorithms and theoretical foundations. MLA-C01 is broader and more practical, with explicit coverage of generative AI workloads on Amazon Bedrock , MLOps patterns, SageMaker JumpStart , and retrieval-augmented generation pipelines. The exam covers four domains: data preparation for machine learning (28%), model development (26%), deployment and orchestration of machine learning workflows (22%), and monitoring, maintenance, and security (24%). That emphasis on deployment and monitoring reflects what employers are actually asking for. They want practitioners who can own a model across its full lifecycle, not just build one. At \$150, this is the most accessible cloud machine learning credential across the three major providers. It correlates with a reported ~20% salary premium and appears consistently in job postings for machine learning engineer and MLOps roles at companies running AWS. A timing note for 2026 readers: AWS has announced that MLA-C01 will be replaced by MLA-C02, which expands to include agentic AI and foundation model workloads. If you're starting prep in late 2026, check AWS's official certification page to confirm which version is currently available. The transition is expected to complete around this article's publication date. Why it's worth it: AWS remains the dominant cloud provider in enterprise machine learning deployments. If your current employer runs on AWS, or you're targeting roles at companies that do, this credential gives you a practical, production-aligned foundation that hiring managers recognize. Best free prep: The official Machine Learning Engineer learning path on AWS Skill Builder . 3. DeepLearning.AI Deep Learning Specialization (Coursera) Cost: ~\$49–59/month via Coursera subscription (roughly \$147–177 over 3 months) | Level: Intermediate | Duration: 3–5 months | Format: Course completion certificate, not a proctored exam Who it's for: Data scientists and machine learning practitioners who want a rigorous, conceptually grounded foundation in deep learning. It's the most widely respected non-vendor certificate available for that purpose. It's worth being precise about what this is and what it isn't. This is a course completion certificate, not a proctored exam-based credential. It doesn't carry the same hiring signal as a Google Cloud or AWS certification. Hiring managers at major tech companies won't be impressed by this certificate on its own. What it does do: it's been taken by more than 960,000 students and carries a 4.9/5.0 rating. Andrew Ng is one of the most credible AI educators around, and the DeepLearning.AI Deep Learning Specialization covers neural network fundamentals, convolutional networks, sequence models, and natural language processing. It's genuinely taught rather than click-through. Employers in the AI and machine learning field recognize the DeepLearning.AI brand, and completing this specialization signals that you've done substantive conceptual work, not just watched promotional videos.

title: Make long-running agents faster with message threads
abstract: Message threads is now available in public beta on the Claude Platform. With message threads, agents no longer need to resend the full conversation history on every turn, reducing latency for long-running sessions. How message threads works A coding agent might make hundreds of requests in one session, and each request resends every earlier message and tool result. Once a conversation reaches hundreds of thousands of tokens, resending all of it adds time before Claude starts responding. With message threads, agents send only what’s new since the last turn, which reduces time to first token (TTFT). With message threads on by default for most Claude Code users, requests with 500k to 1M tokens see median TTFT drop by about 35%. To use message threads, add the thread parameter to Messages API requests. The first request includes the full conversation and starts a thread. Each request after that includes only the new messages and the ID of the previous response. Between turns, we hold each thread in memory, where it’s encrypted and not written to disk. A thread expires 5 minutes after its last request and your client then resends the full conversation to start a new one. While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same. Message threads is best for active sessions where latency matters, including: Long-running coding agents , where each tool result or file edit adds to the conversation. Computer use agents , where screenshots stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn. Document and image-heavy workflows , where requests are made smaller. The more context an agent carries, the more message threads can reduce time to first token. Getting started Message threads is available now in public beta on the native Claude Platform, and on Claude Platform on AWS, Claude in Microsoft Foundry, and on Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed). Standard Claude token rates and existing rate limits apply. See the documentation to get started.

title: Diagnose Distributed AI Workload Failures with NVIDIA Attribution
abstract: In distributed AI workloads, a single error can produce a cascade of symptoms. A GPU or fabric event may surface as NCCL errors on other ranks, scheduler state changes, and thousands of downstream messages. The reported exception shows where the workload stopped, not where the failure began. In this post, you’ll learn how to run NVIDIA Attribution on sample workload evidence, inspect the diagnosis, and explore how attribution rules identify failure patterns. NVIDIA Attribution correlates workload-scoped logs, metrics, telemetry, and scheduler state and returns a structured diagnosis: outcome, root cause, affected nodes, supporting symptoms, and evidence trail. Workload-centric means analyzing failures in the context of a workload rather than as isolated node events. Deterministic rules make the results reproducible and customizable, while structured output enables integration with existing health and recovery systems. NVIDIA health and resilience software helps teams keep AI workloads running. NVIDIA Attribution explains why a workload failed and provides evidence to guide the next action. It complements readiness checks, continuous health monitoring, and the systems that repair infrastructure and restart workloads. NVIDIA Attribution , the workload-centric failure-attribution system used across NVIDIA AI infrastructure, is open source. Used in production across NVIDIA AI infrastructure for years, NVIDIA Attribution analyzes millions of workloads each week across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. In one large RDMA-backed cluster, it correlated port errors, connection resets, and scheduler events to identify patterns around specific host and switch ports, helping teams target fabric repairs and congestion tuning. It includes two deployable components: the NVIDIA Attribution Service and the NVIDIA Attribution Blueprint; both components utilize a core attribution engine. The Service makes attribution available through a RESTAPI; the Blueprint connects cluster schedulers and telemetry sources to the Service and writes the result. Turn workload evidence into one diagnosis NVIDIA Attribution Service analyzes one workload attempt at a time. The Blueprint gathers the workload context and evidence, the Service extracts and correlates events, and the Blueprint returns a structured result. The path has four stages: Scope the workload. The Blueprint identifies the workload attempt from scheduler identifiers or from an explicit execution window and node allocation. Collect observations. Log and metric connectors produce workload-scoped Observation records from application logs, syslogs, GPU driver and Fabric Manager messages, scheduler history, node and network metrics. Extract and correlate events. The Service invokes the attribution engine to identify significant events such as GPU XIDs, NCCL failures, scheduler transitions, and metric conditions. Deterministic rules evaluate their timing and interaction, separate downstream symptoms from the event that caused the failure, and identify the root cause. Return a structured result. The Blueprint combines the verdict with the workload outcome ( terminal_state ), attributed domain ( sub_domain ), symptoms, affected nodes, and a record of collector coverage and errors. From applogs to attribution What follows is a worked example of extracting evidence, interpreting events, and preserving the symptoms that explain a distributed workload failure. Consider a multi-rank training workload in which one GPU encounters a hard fault e.g: XID 149 and NCCL errors follow across other ranks. NVIDIA Attribution correlates events across nodes, identifies the XID as the root cause, retains the NCCL failures in the symptom chain, and names the responsible node. The workload is reported as a hardware failure rather than a set of independent communication errors. A failed collective can leave error reports on several nodes. Those reports tell us where the workload noticed a problem. To explain the failure, NVIDIA Attribution combines them with evidence from other sources and evaluates the symptoms together. In this synthetic workload, application logs contain three different NCCL errors. System logs on node-02 contain XID 149 with error words that decode to NVLink signal integrity issue. We will follow that evidence through the rules pipeline. Interpreting logs with extraction The Extraction phase is the first to run; it runs on the raw input logs and produces structured events to be processed by later stages. Figure 1. Extraction turns application and system logs into typed events with source provenance. These will be processed by later phases in the attribution process Decode NVLink evidence during filtering Filter rules read and write the event stream. The EARLY-stage HandleXidBurstEvents rule reads the XID burst evidence, decodes the error words, and emits an attribution event for signal integrity issue on node-02 . The three NCCL events remain unchanged during this step. Figure 2. EARLY filtering decodes NVLink signal integrity issue while leaving the three NCCL events unchanged Figure 2, above, The figure abbreviates the decoded symptom as XID-149.4 signal integrity issue. The filter also emits parser information for inspection. Refine the symptoms into one attribution The framework materializes events into per-node symptoms, runs per-node scrubbing, and aggregates the surviving symptoms into a job-wide set. In this example, all four candidates reach FINAL refinement. Xid149AndNvlinkFiltering retains the signal integrity symptom and demotes the other node symptoms. Gb200PriorityRootCause reduces the active job-wide symptom set. Outcome mapping then produces the hardware-failure attribution. Figure 3. FINAL refinement surfaces signal integrity issue on node-02 and retains the NCCL reports as interesting evidence The attribution surfaces node-02 and signal integrity issue. The NCCL reports remain useful evidence: demotion preserves their original sources as “interesting,” so they can still be inspected. When multiple causes fit the evidence, sub_domain is ambiguous. Quality of attribution is dependent on the quality and completeness of the underlying telemetry. The diagnosis records that distinction, correctly reflecting uncertainty instead of converting incomplete evidence into a definitive diagnosis. Service and Blueprint architecture Figure 4. NVIDIA Attribution Service and Blueprint architecture diagram showing how the Attribution Blueprint collects workload evidence from scheduler and telemetry sources, passes it to the Attribution Service for analysis, and writes a structured diagnosis to output sinks including a read-only dashboard The attribution engine contains the rules engine and core attribution logic. The Attribution Service exposes that logic through an HTTP API, and the Blueprint handles cluster-specific integration. This separation lets teams apply the same attribution logic across clusters while adapting scheduler, telemetry, and output connectors to each environment. Attribution Service: A self-hosted HTTP wrapper around the core attribution engine that receives normalized observations and returns one verdict for each workload. Attribution Blueprint: A Python reference orchestrator that discovers workloads, resolves the ExecutionContext , runs collectors, calls the Service, enriches the verdict, writes the AttributionBlueprintResult , and supplies a read-only dashboard. This is intended to be a reference implementation for practitioners to customize the solution to their environment. The Blueprint ships with: Execution-context connectors for Slurm , Kueue , and static inputs Log and metric connectors for Loki , local files, Kubernetes pod logs, and PromQL metrics Output connectors for stdout and SQLite Blueprints can run near each cluster’s data sources, with either a dedicated Attribution Service for each Blueprint or a shared Service for multiple Blueprints.

title: Keep Distributed Training Running with Automated Workload Recovery
abstract: As distributed AI training scales, failures across hardware and software dependencies increasingly disrupt training progress, making fast, reliable recovery essential. A stalled training rank can trigger an NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) timeout, a GPU node can stop responding to the scheduler, or a straggler can slow the entire job. Each disruption is manageable on its own, but the cumulative impact and recovery overhead determine how efficiently the system converts wall-clock time into productive training progress or goodput . Manual recovery becomes unsustainable when it must cover every training job across a cluster, around the clock, at scale. Each interruption demands log analysis, fault isolation, and a restart from a saved checkpoint, while affected GPUs remain idle during recovery. As the number and size of training jobs grow, overlapping failures increase the engineering burden and wasted GPU-hours. Without continuous coverage, those losses can accumulate, increasing overall compute costs and extending time to train. NVIDIA Recovery , part of NVIDIA DSX OS , the modular software portfolio with the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , is an open-source, workload-level service that automates recovery across a cluster’s training jobs, around the clock. It detects interruptions using application logs, GPU metrics, and scheduler signals, uses failure attribution to identify implicated resources, and coordinates isolation and checkpoint restarts from checkpoints on healthy capacity. By automating this recovery loop across workloads, it handles concurrent interruptions, reduces manual intervention, and helps sustain training goodput. This post explains how the recovery loop works, how NVIDIA Recovery integrates with Slurm , and how to deploy it on your own cluster. Workload recovery is a distinct AI factory concern Our previous NVIDIA DGX Cloud resilience post , GTC talk and NVIDIA Mission Control 2.5 post describe a layered approach to keeping training productive. NVIDIA Recovery builds on that architecture by connecting infrastructure remediation to workload recovery. Break-fix automation identifies faulty nodes, removes them from service, and routes hardware for remediation. Framework-level libraries such as NVRx provide recovery, hang detection, and straggler mitigation within individual training jobs, but each user must configure and manage these capabilities for their own workloads. Cluster workload managers such as Slurm manage resource allocation, queuing, and container execution. Workload recovery is a distinct coordination problem: restoring productive training requires attributing failures to their causes, deciding whether and where affected jobs should restart, and acting consistently across workloads that share infrastructure. Addressing this problem requires a cluster-level control loop that integrates infrastructure remediation, framework-level recovery, and cluster workload management, with operational metrics that track recovery latency, recovery success rate, and time to restore productive training. Multi-level NVIDIA health and resilience stack As shown in Figure 1, below, NVIDIA Recovery provides the dedicated workload recovery layer within the DSX OS Stack . Node health monitoring and isolation depend on the cluster’s orchestration and workload management stack. Kubernetes deployments use NVSentinel to monitor GPU health metrics and XID events and automatically cordon and drain faulty nodes. Many Slurm sites check node health with custom prolog and epilog scripts. The slurm-operator from the Slinky project natively supports and injects these same scripts when running Slurm on Kubernetes. Within individual training jobs, NVRx provides a library for in-job recovery and hang detection. NVIDIA Recovery coordinates recovery across workloads at the cluster level , integrating with these capabilities to manage job restarts, placement, and node exclusion. Figure 1. NVIDIA Recovery’s role in health and resilience integration These layers operate independently without hard dependencies, allowing you to adopt each modular component or plug in your own platform component to integrate. For example, if your cluster already relies on NVSentinel or NVIDIA Health Validation, you can integrate NVIDIA Recovery with little or no changes to your existing health workflows. For environments already running NVRx, NVIDIA Recovery fills the gap that in-job restart cannot reach by managing the cross-workload lifecycle and node exclusion. When paired with NVIDIA Attribution, it receives rich cross-layer diagnostic verdicts that enrich the persistent audit trail. Cost of the gap At cluster scale, rare per-GPU failures compound. Even if each GPU operates without failure on a given day with 99.9% probability, a job spanning 10,000 GPUs completes that day uninterrupted with a probability of only 0.999 10,000 ≈ 0.005%. This explains why, in an 11-month study of 24,000 A100 GPUs at Meta , hardware failures interrupted fewer than 1% of jobs while those jobs accounted for 19% of GPU runtime: the largest, longest-running jobs are the most exposed. NVIDIA Recovery automates recovery across a cluster’s training workloads, and is useful for both small and large distributed runs. Across many smaller jobs, interruptions accumulate, increasing the operational burden. In large jobs, each interruption affects more GPUs, amplifying the compute cost of recovery. Automated recovery addresses both challenges. Our production observations underscore the need for such efficient, automated recovery that scales across cluster workloads: from July 9 to Oct. 9, NVIDIA Recovery monitoring on one training cluster covered nearly 200 jobs per day and recorded approximately 8,550 anomaly detections, with mean detection and recovery-action latencies of 69 and 94 seconds, respectively. This unattended, cluster-wide response reduces dependence on individual engineers and per-user recovery arrangements as interruptions accumulate. Recovery-action latency ends at the automated action; scheduling and checkpoint restoration determine when productive training resumes. The automated recovery loop NVIDIA Recovery coordinates recovery across the cluster’s training workloads. Four stages organize the loop, with actions determined by the interruption and configured policy: Detect : The Anomaly Detector combines application logs and scheduler signals to identify crashes, hangs, and stragglers. It recognizes PyTorch and NCCL failures, CUDA errors, and interconnect failure patterns. Missing progress signals or recognized communication-hang patterns indicate potential hangs; sustained throughput degradation relative to a recent baseline indicates potential stragglers. Attribute : NVIDIA Recovery uses the scheduler signals and application logs gathered during detection to classify the interruption and guide recovery actions. Optional integration with NVIDIA Attribution adds deeper diagnosis to distinguish hardware faults, system-software issues, and application bugs. This evidence informs node exclusion and enriches the audit trail. Operators can also integrate their own attribution service and adopt NVIDIA Recovery independently. Isolate: The Anomaly Remediator applies the recovery recommendation, excluding implicated nodes from subsequent restart attempts or stopping the workload when further retries would be unproductive. It tracks implicated nodes across attempts to avoid recurring failures. In addition, a safety net (watchdog service) allows normal scheduling to proceed if a recovery decision takes too long or outright fails, preventing workloads from waiting indefinitely. Restart or Stop : The scheduler integration acts on NVIDIA Recovery’s recommendation through the Advisor API to restart the workload or stop unproductive retries. On restart, the application resumes from its last saved checkpoint using its existing restart logic.

title: Making Kubernetes AI-Ready for NVIDIA Vera Rubin on Day One
abstract: Configuring and optimizing Kubernetes for new GPU hardware such as NVIDIA Vera Rubin is complex and error-prone. Drivers, kernels, runtimes, networking, operators, and schedulers must work together, with settings tuned to the hardware and workload. Small mismatches can prevent workloads from running or limit performance. The NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) —part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform —simplifies this work by capturing tuned configurations in reusable recipes, generating bundles for existing deployment tools, and validating the running cluster. It will help Kubernetes environments be ready for NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 compute trays on Day 1. Overall, the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together technologies to help the ecosystem design, build, and operate more efficient AI factories, including open source, modular software components purpose-built to support multi-tenant operations and scaling. Configuring new hardware architecture in a cloud-native stack requires plumbing updates from the lowest-level bindings all the way up to the orchestration layer. It is still early days for Vera Rubin. This post covers what changes if you run NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 today, what has been validated on early hardware access using NVIDIA GPU Operator and the Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) driver with Vera Rubin support. It also shows how AICR brings these components together in a configuration that platform teams can reproduce and verify. What changes from GB200 NVL72: planning your upgrade If you run GB200 NVL72 today, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 is an evolution of the same NVIDIA MGX rack-scale architecture, now in its third generation. But several user-visible pieces change. Knowing about them now lets you plan cluster software and configuration changes alongside upcoming releases: GPU driver: Vera Rubin NVL72 requires a new driver branch. It has been validated with R615.23, the host-installed R615.23 open GPU driver. Early support is targeted for R610, with official platform support in R620. AICR’s GB200 baseline is R580.173.02. R615.23 is the current tested version, not a confirmed minimum for official Vera Rubin support. DOCA and NIC drivers: Vera Rubin NVL72 replaces the GB200 NVL72 reference design’s NVIDIA ConnectX-7 NICs and NVIDIA BlueField-3 data processing units (DPUs) with NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs and NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs . DOCA 3.3.0 is the first GA release supporting ConnectX-9. The Vera Rubin system image validated on ships DOCA-OFED 3.3.0. This is the testbed version, not a requirement or a recommendation. AICR uses host-installed NIC drivers and DRANET for pod allocation here. Network Operator compatibility remains a separate qualification step (See the DOCA 3.3.0 release notes ). Device topology: The NIC/GPU/Direct Memory Access (DMA) topology of the Vera Rubin NVL72 compute tray differs from GB200, so GPU-to-NIC affinity and NUMA placement must be checked for I/O-intensive workloads such as Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) networking and GPUDirect Storage. Both reference trays contain two CPUs and four GPUs, but the Vera Rubin NVL72 trays expose eight ConnectX-9 PCI device groups with 32 functions, compared with four ConnectX-7 adapters on the NVIDIA DGX GB200 NVL72 compute tray. In both GB200 NVL72 and Vera Rubin NVL72 trays, GPUs 0 to 1 have CPU NUMA affinity 0; GPUs 2 to 3 have affinity 1. GPU-to-NIC connectivity is NODE within a socket and SYS across sockets. PCI function counts do not represent physical port counts (See the GB200 reference architecture ). IMEX: As on GB200 NVL72, multi-node NVIDIA NVLink workloads use IMEX. With DRA-managed IMEX, stop, disable, and mask the host’s static nvidia-imex service to prevent ownership conflicts. DRA v0.5.0 adds an alpha host-managed option with domain isolation only; our cluster uses driverManaged mode. (See the release notes ) NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) profiles: Rubin GPUs introduce new MIG profiles. R615.23 advertises these profiles on node. The AICR Vera Rubin recipes use whole-GPU allocation and do not configure MIG. MIG on Vera Rubin is not covered by this validation. AICR recipes: All of these deltas are encoded in the new Vera Rubin recipe family, so aicr recipe and aicr validate reflect the validated combination rather than leaving you to rediscover each change (details are in the following sections). Validation on Vera Rubin NVL72 To validate Vera Rubin NVL72 support end to end, we deployed the AICR runtime bundle on Vera Rubin clusters using the official GPU Operator v26.7.0 release and the official DRA driver v0.5.0 release, with a host-installed R615 driver. Both the training and inference recipe variants now validate end to end for deployment and conformance. For training, an initial performance gate: a cross-node NCCL all-reduce over the NVIDIA NVLink fabric, running through an IMEX ComputeDomain and gated on a bus-bandwidth floor. GPU pods run cleanly, and IMEX channels are injected into claiming pods across multiple nodes, shown with real cluster output below. A note on early-silicon realities: Bringing up new silicon is a process. The first validation rounds were temporarily blocked by a hardware/fabric issue in one of the early Vera Rubin clusters—unrelated to the GPU Operator or the DRA driver—that kept one compute tray out of the NVLink fabric. After the hardware was reseated, all GPUs on both nodes joined a single clean fabric clique. From bring-up to reproducible recipes Validating the components is only half the story. Standing up a working Vera Rubin cluster means choosing driver mode, container-runtime wiring, component versions, and a handful of platform-specific settings. AICR captures those choices as a versioned recipe, so the configuration on real Vera Rubin hardware is explicit, reproducible, and verifiable across clusters. The new Vera Rubin recipe family (service: rke2; accelerator: Vera Rubin NVL72 (vr200); operating system: Ubuntu; with training, inference, and NVIDIA Dynamo inference variants) ships as Preview. It’s an early-adopter path that does not yet carry the production support and lifecycle qualification of a Supported recipe while the platform itself is pre-release. It encodes the decisions made during this bring-up: Host-managed driver: The Vera Rubin system image pre-installs the arm64 open-kernel-module driver, so the recipe runs the GPU Operator with driver.enabled: false , while the container toolkit stays operator-managed. The recipe moves to the operator-managed driver when the official builds ship. DRA driver with ComputeDomains: IMEX-backed ComputeDomains are enabled for the NVL72 fabric, with whole-GPU allocation remaining on the device plugin. Platform floors and quirks: They’re encoded once so users don’t rediscover them. Kubernetes >= 1.34.1 — 1.34 for the GA resource.k8s.io/v1 DRA API that ComputeDomains/IMEX use, and the .1 patch because the RKE2 CDI/NRI toolkit path needs containerd 2.1 (v1.34.1+rke2r1). Ubuntu 26.04 with the Vera-optimized arm64 64k-page kernel. And smaller sharp edges, such as raising the NFD topology updater’s default 60Mi memory limit, which out of memory (OOM) kills on multi-terabyte NVL72 workers. The first deployment of this bundle targeted a platform combination none of these components had ever been validated on together—arm64, Ubuntu 26.04, a 64k-page kernel, RKE2, and Vera Rubin—and went from cluster handoff to a healthy runtime in hours. A second Vera Rubin cluster reproduced the result the following day, and that repeatability is the point and benefit of the recipe. The workflow on a live Vera Rubin cluster To make this concrete, here is the actual AICR workflow, executed on a live Vera Rubin NVL72 reference cluster with the AICR v1.0.0 toolchain. 1. Generate the recipe Recipe generation is offline: It resolves criteria against the recipe catalog and takes seconds. $ aicr recipe \ --service rke2 \ --accelerator vr200 \ --os ubuntu \ --intent training \ -o recipe.

title: Build World Models for Interactive Simulation with NVIDIA Cosmos
abstract:
Physical AI developers working with world models face two distinct challenges: adapting models to their sensors, tasks, and data, and getting those models into applications reliably. NVIDIA Cosmos addresses each. Cosmos is a platform of world foundation models and development tools for physical AI . Cosmos Framework provides agent skills and recipes for world model training, multimodal data processing, optimization and inference. Cosmos NIM microservices supports GPU-accelerated serving through application APIs. This post walks through both. The simulation section shows how to use Cosmos Framework’s inference recipes and agent skills to generate synchronized camera video and LiDAR observations for AV, robot, and surgical scenarios, starting from released checkpoints you can run today. The deployment section shows how to choose a NIM configuration for your GPU, launch the container, verify readiness, and send your first inference request. When to use Cosmos Framework for world model development Cosmos Framework is an open and fully modular framework for world model training, model optimization, and inference to support a full model development lifecycle using new agent skills. It is expanding beyond Cosmos 3 to support NVIDIA Alpamayo , GR00T, Qwen, pi0.5, and other compatible Hugging Face models. Training Train models on text, images, video, audio, and actions faster using new skills. Use LoRA for parameter-efficient adaptation, or full supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to update all model parameters. Load data through JSONL, WebDataset, LeRobot, or custom adapters and train across GPUs and save checkpoints to resume runs. Point your agent to post-training skill to accelerate and automate. Apply Reinforcement Learning The platform now covers online and offline RL paths . Newly supported pipelines include: DPO: offline preference optimization. GRPO: online RL with a rule or model reward and vLLM rollouts. PPO: actor-critic RL with frozen reference and critic, including RL for embodied policies in simulation. OPD: on-policy distillation from a frozen teacher. DiffusionNFT: online RL for diffusion world models. Run rollout, reward, and training roles on shared GPUs or separate pools. Connect supported simulators to collect experience. Optimize models and inference Distill models to reduce model size or generation steps; quantize models to reduce memory use. Run compatible checkpoints with Hugging Face Diffusers, PyTorch, SGLang, vLLM-Omni, vLLM, TRT-LLM and TRT-Edge-LLM or NVIDIA NIM. Evaluate for quality, accuracy and GPU usage and maximize compute utilization. Use agents with Cosmos Framework Load the setup, inference, post-training, and troubleshooting skills under .agents/skills . Give the agent a bounded task: Prompt : Post-train <checkpoint> on <dataset> using <recipe> . Pin all revisions, validate the dataset, and keep training and evaluation episodes separate. Run the smoke test, save the configuration, and stop at <N> GPU-hours. Export and compare against the base model on held-out data using three seeds. Repeat evaluation at a supported lower precision; record quality, peak memory, and latency. Which Cosmos simulation workflow should you use? Cosmos Framework provides post-training and inference recipes for robot simulation, realistic scene generation, multi-camera driving simulation, and surgical policy evaluation. New Cosmos 3 Nano simulation recipes and example checkpoints enable developers to use agent runnable skills to evaluate our example checkpoints and adapt Cosmos 3 Nano to custom sensors, action space, and data domains. These checkpoints support PyTorch and vLLM-Omni, tested on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs. Use the recipe to select GPU count, memory configuration, and inference settings. Autonomous vehicle simulation: Both AV checkpoints take a prompt and World Scenario Map (WSM) controls representing lanes, objects, road markings, traffic signs, and road boundaries. Joint RGB–LiDAR generation additionally uses HD-map rangemap controls and supports optional initial LiDAR observations. Prompts describe weather, lighting, time of day, road conditions with prefixes providing camera-rig and field-of-view context. An optional initial camera images provide visual context to guide the generated scene’s appearance. Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto uses bidirectional generation to denoise an entire multi-view clip at once for offline synthetic data generation . It supports 30 fps input and output video, with up to 400 frames at 480p or 720p; longer sequences can be generated through autoregressive chunking. Change the prompt to turn a daytime drive into a rainy night while keeping the same road layout and vehicle trajectories. Use these variations to train and evaluate perception and driving models across weather and lighting conditions. After Framework setup, run the four-GPU examples below from the repository root. For Transfer-Auto, use the published sample configuration with seven synchronized WSM videos, per-camera captions, first-frame RGB conditioning, and HD-map LiDAR controls. See the Transfer-Auto inference guide for setup, input preparation, and output details. export COSMOS_TRAINING=0 COSMOS_INTERNAL=0 hf download nvidia/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto \ --local-dir checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto AUTO_SAMPLE_ROOT="$PWD/checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto/assets/sample_data"
AUTO_NEGATIVE_PROMPT="$(cat .agents/skills/cosmos3-nano-transfer-auto/inference/assets/negative-prompt.txt)" torchrun --standalone --nproc-per-node=4 \ -m cosmos_framework.scripts.inference \ -i "$AUTO_SAMPLE_ROOT/input-transfer-auto.jsonl" \ -o outputs/transfer_auto \ --checkpoint-path checkpoints/Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto \ --resolution 720 --num-steps 35 \ --per-view-negative-prompt "$AUTO_NEGATIVE_PROMPT" \ --cp-size 4 --cfgp-size 1 \ --no-use-torch-compile --no-diffusion-cache The reference run produces seven 720p videos (297 frames at 30 FPS) and 99 LiDAR sweeps. Check sample_outputs.json for success and lidar.safetensors for finite range and intensity values, then verify WSM alignment and consistency across camera views and LiDAR. For custom scenarios and rig adaptation, see the WSM renderer and Transfer-Auto post-training guides . For point-cloud conversion and visualization, see the LiDAR visualization utilities Video 1. Surround-view video and LiDAR generation with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causal, few-step-distilled variant of Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto, enabling autoregressive streaming generation. It generates observations incrementally as an AV policy or human driving input updates the scenario through a WSM renderer.
