title: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights
abstract: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room. People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display . The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028. The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.

title: Claude’s new rules against game cloning won’t stop the AI copying boom
abstract: Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it's unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months. A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name "chasm" was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name "tengu_heron_brook"—reads as follows: Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original. XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30 . XDA also reported that the "tengu_heron_brook" rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle.

title: Scott Alexander’s Against SURA Seems Deeply Confused
abstract: If you are helping build something that might kill everyone, maybe stop doing that. Ideally, when you do stop, tell everyone else to also stop building it. That is certainly the obvious, first-level thing to do. You need a damn good reason to decide that no, actually you should keep building the thing that might kill everyone. Scott Alexander is worried too many people are insisting upon this too loudly. He comes out against a strategy focused on getting people to stop. I disagree. I think many of the claims, arguments and rhetoric in Scott’s post are quite poor by the standards that Scott Alexander would apply to himself. Scott clearly continues to support advocacy for a global pause, or what he calls Plan A. His objection is to those advocating primarily or exclusively for SURA, which stands for ‘stop unilaterally and raise awareness.’ The practical differences here are smaller than they may at first appear. This post first lays out my understanding of Scott Alexander’s core claims, then gives my core reactions to those claims, then goes over various questions in detail along with gathering the resulting discussions. Scott Alexander writes Against SURA , or the strategy of calling upon nations and companies building superintelligence to stop building it and calling upon employees of those labs to quit, even without reciprocity. Here is his definition and coinage: I’ll lump these ideas together under the heading of “SURA” – the idea that the only ethical course is for people/companies/countries to Stop Unilaterally + Raise Awareness, with no plan for what happens if race dynamics continue anyway. I interpret the planks of SURA’s platform as: I mostly avoid quoting directly from the OP , since most of you likely read it. Scott’s basic frame of the situation is that there are two classes of plan: Scott’s core arguments are that (this is my ITT summary of Scott): Scott also makes other claims, such as his overview of alignment. In many cases the claims seem overgeneralized or overstated. I respond to Scott’s claims, and without any implicit endorsement of claims I do not mention. It is not Scott’s main point, but I want to flag that I strongly disagree with Scott’s stated model of alignment. I do not believe that AI models are well-modeled as ‘inheriting virtue’ simply because they learn to imitate humans. If nothing else, this implies that AI base models are “virtuous” until you “corrupt” them with RLVR. No. This is at best highly misleading. This was a plausible candidate for the worst thing in the post. I do agree with Scott’s general theory of what Plan C alignment success looks like, in that it involves trying to string prosaic stopgaps together long enough to let the AI pivot to doing our alignment homework for us, and hopefully its alignment can become self-reinforcing and antifragile. I agree that this seems potentially possible, but I also think it is very easy to see multiple places where a p(doom) of 90%+ could come from, including: The most obvious and common reason for a very high p(doom) is to believe, in the style of Eliezer Yudkowsky, that alignment requires you to hit a very precise target, on the first try, while dodging a rather large List of Lethalities . They argue that asking AIs to automate the alignment research will inevitably mean they miss key elements or otherwise fail. I think that is super reasonable, and it is strange to me that Scott Alexander finds this hard to understand. This exchange has some abridged responses. Oliver Habryka: But yeah, I think you should obviously be willing to risk war if a foreign lab is working towards building ASI. Scott Alexander : I think these considerations apply in a small fraction of worlds where the US government is very alignment-pilled but China isn’t. … Under my model a really good Plan C+ has an 90%+ chance of working. Oliver Habryka : God man, I really find it extremely wild to think that we will solve the alignment problem with an expected 6-12 month lead, in a unilateral fashion and thereafter declare the end of history. This just seems so incredibly wild to me, and you are pursuing a strategy where you and your friends are building the machine gods unilaterally betting all you have on it. Scott Alexander : My reasoning in coming up with that number was that my unconditional p(doom) is 25%, and since a really good Plan C+ is a much better world than I expect in real life, it’s probably a little less than half that. Oliver Habryka: You don’t need to be “entirely united around solving the alignment problem” in order to think it’s a bad idea to build god-like machine intelligence. This is the whole central point I keep making. Countries have lots of reasons to think that it’s super bad news for other countries to go and build very powerful AI systems. The default outcome is that countries will try to prevent other countries from doing that, using existing tools of international diplomacy and escalation (and probably also using new AI technologies themselves). The level of buy-in necessary to start telling other countries to not do fucking crazy stuff is vastly vastly less than the level of buy-in necessary to “be entirely united around solving the alignment problem”. Indeed, I have trouble seeing a world where you don’t get enormous buy-in in basically every country in the world as military applications of AI start being widespread. You don’t get to start out with an unconditional p(doom) at the bottom of the page and then reason from that, or all you are doing is restating the 25%. At best this is an intuition pump. Also I find the idea that AI goes well 90% of the time on a C+ style plan to be pretty absurdist. There are multiple distinct steps that seem much more likely than this to go wrong under such conditions. This 90% is also 30%+ above every source Scott cites on this question. I mean, yes, obviously if you think that a prosaic and time pressured but reasonably executed plan has a 90%+ chance of success, then given the current state of the world your primary strategy should be to try and navigate to such a scenario. I would love, love, love to lock in a 90% success rate. Obviously that is an ‘unacceptable risk’ but there is no better alternative on offer. Scott is not actually advocating for full abandonment of Plan A in favor of Plan C, only coming out against those who would abandon Plan C for Plan A, which to me represents a substantially lower probability of success than 90% for a Plan C+. If you believe there is no deontological prohibition against building a thing that might kill everyone, you don’t believe in deontological prohibitions. Which is fine. You can decide not to believe in them. But then say that. One can also say that there are times when you must do deontologically evil things in the service of a greater good, despite them being deontologically evil. Again, this is fine, and I even agree with you. But then say that. The same applies to virtue ethics arguments, which look similar in such cases. Certainly one must do some things that contribute to some other bad things. This is especially true if one counts engagement in trade that indirectly rewards efforts that also point towards other bad outcomes, despite the product you buy itself being good and causing good outcomes, or your actions incidentally providing tiny marginal funding for things that already have vast funding. One cannot go around never doing anything that is at all entangled with things that have negative consequences. One cannot count only the negative consequences of one’s actions, including indirect ones, and ignore the positive. That’s Asymmetric Justice, as I discussed in 2019 , and it is incompatible with survival or civilization. There must exist ethical consumption under capitalism and also under other systems, especially consumption that enables your productivity in good causes. Ultimately one must talk price.

title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
abstract: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude’s new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total—the surveyed group (a “panel”) cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: For comparison, here’s that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered “yes” around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in “producing goods or services”. Under the new “any business function” wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered “yes” around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the “Employment size class” XLSX file, available from here . Here’s a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses—here’s my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here’s the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more “producing goods or services”—now it’s “in any of its business functions”! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn’t find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 . The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording—the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn’t going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out “formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI”. I can’t help but laugh at the absurdity of “SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service” though. This is The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence” by Simon Willison, posted on 2nd November 2026 . title: Building AI for Lawyers - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
abstract: In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work. Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO. Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year. We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → When Jacob first read Leya's YC application, he had one piece of feedback: people had tried building legal tech a million times, and it never worked. If lawyers bill by the hour, getting faster means earning less. Why would they buy a tool that does that? What changed, he says, is the pressure on firms. In the US, routine work like small reviews is already shifting to flat project fees. Some firms do it for free to hold on to the client. The money moves to M&A, litigation, and time spent with clients. We asked whether that means firms will stop needing paralegals and junior lawyers. Jacob says that's not what Legora is seeing. A good junior is worth more today than two years ago because they get so much more done, just as in engineering. Jump to the billing model discussion → Most teams improve their agents by reading traces. Legora can't read any. Almost everything users upload is confidential, and much of it belongs to the firm's clients, not the firm. So the evals team has to recreate the kinds of work customers do. Three engineers and three lawyers build RL environments to simulate the work their customers do. One example is a 10,000-file data room where the agent runs due diligence and has to produce a report that catches the right red flags. The team plots the results on a heat map by practice area and task. A new model often gets better at some kinds of legal work and worse at others. The team draws on a pool of about 100 legal engineers: lawyers who spent three or four years in big law, often with a CS degree. In production, Legora classifies failures into 10 to 20 known failure modes and runs cheap LLM-based checks behind feature flags. Those restrictions also determine which infrastructure Legora can use. Everything runs on Azure because when Legora started, law firms wouldn't accept AWS or GCP, and Microsoft was already an approved vendor through 365. Jump to evals without traces → Legora resisted a model picker for a long time before giving in. Jacob's view is that a lawyer shouldn't have to decide whether a contract is a Sonnet-high or an Opus-mid task. It's Legora's job to find the best available tradeoff between quality, cost, latency, governance, and regional availability. He estimates that models already handle about 60% of legal work really well. For those tasks it's a cost and latency problem now. Complex analysis and editing across million-token contracts still need more intelligence. Legora has started post-training open-weight models for narrow tasks like legal research, with no plans to train its own frontier model. For drafting, Jacob finds Fable and Opus too verbose. Astra is more concise. To address hallucinations, everything the agent writes gets a citation that highlights a bounding box in the source PDF, multiple layers down. Jump to the model discussion → Six months into the job, Jacob showed the team a slide of the 300 Spartans and declared that Legora would stay at 20 engineers forever. It now has 100, and he says that still feels too small. His job now is to build a system where the team can ship just a few things and customers feel like they're getting a lot. The team builds around a few primitives: projects that hold files, the agent, Tabular Review, and lists. Lists are a flexible Notion-style database with triggers and automations. Agents can create and read lists, and changes to a list can start an agent. Intake is a Slack bot that turns a request into a ticket on a list. Tabular Review is the one the industry copied, down to the name. Each row is a document, each column is a question. Drop in 10,000 employment contracts and ask for the termination period, the IP assignment clause, and the severance terms. It supports up to a million cells, but starts with just 10 rows so you can fix your prompts before running the rest. Legal engineers configure new products on these primitives without writing code. Even Wexler's fact intelligence product runs on the same building blocks. Jump to the primitives discussion → Legora hired its first forward deployed engineer about nine months ago in New York: Di Qi, a two-time YC founder who worked on search at Meta. Legal engineers configure the product the way a power user would and don't write code. Forward deployed engineers write code into production, build integrations into a firm's CRM or document management system, and push what they learn back into the core product. They still don't touch client data. When a big, engaged client signs, Legora assigns legal engineers to work with them and adds an FDE if the project needs one. Within a year, Jacob expects to have a rotating group of FDEs who sit with a client for a couple of months, build what they need, and move on. Jump to the forward deployed discussion → In two years, Jacob thinks big enterprises will use Legora through tools like Claude Cowork, while law firms work inside Legora directly. He doesn't expect the labs to cut Legora off the way they've done to coding companies. For a $400 million M&A deal, he thinks people will still want Legora. Legora — the collaborative AI platform for lawyers, where Jacob is CTO. Jacob Lauritzen — Jacob on LinkedIn. Legora's Series E announcement — $550 million at an $8.8 billion valuation, with ARR above $200 million. "Agents need more than a chat" — Jacob's talk at AI Engineer Europe 2026. "Connect AI to Billions of Legal Documents" — Jacob's AI Engineer talk with Simon Eskildsen of turbopuffer. How Legora runs 2,000 parallel agent evals on Modal Sandboxes — the infrastructure behind Legora's eval runs. Legora acquires Qura — the Stockholm legal research startup Legora bought in April. Legora is acquiring Wexler — the London startup that extracts and verifies facts across large litigation document sets. Claude for Legal — Anthropic's legal connectors and plugins, the backdrop to whether the labs will come for legal. AIE Europe Debrief + Agent Labs Thesis — Swyx on the agent lab playbook he brings up at the start. • 0:00 Cold open • 0:40 Meet Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora • 1:05 Starting out as underdogs in a Stockholm basement • 1:54 How Legora grew from ChatGPT with Swedish law into a legal agent • 4:12 The switch from assistant to agent • 5:23 Which models Legora uses and why it added a model picker • 7:48 Are today’s models good enough for lawyers?

title: Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
abstract: Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence. • Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one • Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model • How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning • A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything. • Why Legora runs everything on Azure and why it doesn’t use ElevenLabs • Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name • How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent • What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code • The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. Now there are 100, and he still feels short-handed. • Why Jacob finds Fable and Opus too chatty for drafting and likes Astra’s concise writing • Why drafting a long contract is a search problem • Whether model labs will cut off legal tools the way they cut off coding tools • What happens to law firm partnerships, the billable hour, and jobs for junior lawyers Legora is hiring engineers in New York, Stockholm, and London. 0:40 Meet Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora 1:05 Starting out as underdogs in a Stockholm basement 1:54 How Legora grew from ChatGPT with Swedish law into a legal agent 4:12 The switch from assistant to agent 5:23 Which models Legora uses and why it added a model picker 7:48 Are today’s models good enough for lawyers? title: karpathy/nanochat
abstract:
nanochat nanochat is the simplest experimental harness for training LLMs. It is designed to run on a single GPU node, the code is minimal/hackable, and it covers all major LLM stages including tokenization, pretraining, finetuning, evaluation, and inference. For example, you can train your own GPT-2 capability LLM (which cost ~$43,000 to train in 2019) for only $48 (~2 hours of 8XH100 GPU node) and then talk to it over a simple CLI. On a spot instance, the total cost can be closer to ~$15. More generally, nanochat is configured out of the box to train an entire miniseries of compute-optimal models by setting one single complexity dial: --depth , the number of layers in the GPT transformer model (GPT-2 capability happens to be approximately depth 26). All other hyperparameters (the width of the transformer, number of heads, learning rate adjustments, training horizons, weight decays, ...) are calculated automatically in an optimal way. For questions about the repo, I recommend either using DeepWiki from Devin/Cognition to ask questions about the repo, or use the Discussions tab , or come by the #nanochat channel on Discord. Time-to-GPT-2 Leaderboard Presently, the main focus of development is on tuning the pretraining stage, which takes the most amount of compute. Inspired by the modded-nanogpt repo and to incentivise progress and community collaboration, nanochat maintains a leaderboard for a "GPT-2 speedrun", which is the wall-clock time required to train a nanochat model to GPT-2 grade capability, as measured by the DCLM CORE score. The runs/speedrun.sh script always reflects the reference way to train GPT-2 grade model and talk to it. The current leaderboard looks as follows: # time val_bpb CORE Description Date Commit Contributors 0 168 hours - 0.2565 Original OpenAI GPT-2 checkpoint 2019 - OpenAI 1 3.04 0.74833 0.2585 d24 baseline, slightly overtrained Jan 29 2026 348fbb3 @karpathy 2 2.91 0.74504 0.2578 d26 slightly undertrained +fp8 Feb 2 2026 a67eba3 @karpathy 3 2.76 0.74645 0.2602 bump total batch size to 1M tokens Feb 5 2026 2c062aa @karpathy 4 2.02 0.71854 0.2571 change dataset to NVIDIA ClimbMix Mar 4 2026 324e69c @ddudek @karpathy 5 1.80 0.71808 0.2690 autoresearch round 1 Mar 9 2026 6ed7d1d @karpathy 6 1.65 0.71800 0.2626 autoresearch round 2 Mar 14 2026 a825e63 @karpathy The primary metric we care about is "time to GPT-2" - the wall clock time needed to outperform the GPT-2 (1.6B) CORE metric on an 8XH100 GPU node. The GPT-2 CORE score is 0.256525. In 2019, the training of GPT-2 cost approximately $43,000 so it is incredible that due to many advances over 7 years across the stack, we can now do so much faster and for well below $100 (e.g. at the current ~$3/GPU/hr, an 8XH100 node is ~$24/hr, so 2 hours is ~$48). See dev/LEADERBOARD.md for more docs on how to interpret and contribute to the leaderboard. Getting started Setup nanochat uses uv for dependency management. To install: uv sync --extra gpu # Use for CUDA (A100/H100/etc.) uv sync --extra cpu # (or) Use for CPU-only / MPS source .venv/bin/activate For development (adds pytest, matplotlib, ipykernel, transformers, etc.): uv sync --extra gpu --group dev Reproduce and talk to GPT-2 The most fun you can have is to train your own GPT-2 and talk to it. The entire pipeline to do so is contained in the single file runs/speedrun.sh , which is designed to be run on an 8XH100 GPU node. Boot up a new 8XH100 GPU box from your favorite provider (e.g. I use and like Lambda ), and kick off the training script: bash runs/speedrun.sh You may wish to do so in a screen session as this will take ~1.5 hours to run. Once it's done, you can talk to your model over the CLI. Make sure again that your local uv virtual environment is active (run source .venv/bin/activate ), and chat: python -m scripts.chat_cli Get it to write stories or poems. Ask it to tell you who you are to see a hallucination. Ask it why the sky is blue. Or why it's green. The speedrun is a 4e19 FLOPs capability model so it's a bit like talking to a kindergartener :). An example conversation with a speedrun model: User: Hello whats up? Assistant: Hello! How can I help you today? User: Why is the sky blue? Assistant: The sky is blue due to an optical illusion called the Rayleigh Scattering of Light, which occurs when sunlight passes through tiny particles in the air. These particles are made up of tiny blue and violet particles that cause the light to bend in a particular way. User: That's cool. Write a poem about it. Assistant: In the twilight's glow, the sky is blue, A canvas of shimmering blue, where skies unfold, A world of blue, where blue and more blue, Are woven together in a tapestry so fine, Where every hue seems to sing a story. ... A few more notes: The code will run just fine on the Ampere 8XA100 GPU node as well, but a bit slower. All code will run just fine on even a single GPU by omitting torchrun , and will produce ~identical results (code will automatically switch to gradient accumulation), but you'll have to wait 8 times longer. If your GPU(s) have less than 80GB, you'll have to tune some of the hyperparameters or you will OOM / run out of VRAM. Look for --device-batch-size in the scripts and reduce it until things fit. E.g. from 32 (default) to 16, 8, 4, 2, or even 1. Less than that you'll have to know a bit more what you're doing and get more creative. Most of the code is fairly vanilla PyTorch so it should run on anything that supports that - xpu, mps, or etc, but I haven't personally exercised all of these code paths so there might be sharp edges. Research If you are a researcher and wish to help improve nanochat, two scripts of interest are runs/scaling_laws.sh and runs/miniseries.sh . See Jan 7 miniseries v1 for related documentation. For quick experimentation (~5 min pretraining runs) my favorite scale is to train a 12-layer model (GPT-1 sized), e.g. like this: OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 torchrun --standalone --nproc_per_node=8 -m scripts.base_train -- \
    --depth=12 \
    --run="d12" \
    --model-tag="d12" \
    --core-metric-every=999999 \
    --sample-every=-1 \
    --save-every=-1 \ This uses wandb (run name "d12"), only runs the CORE metric on last step, and it doesn't sample and save intermediate checkpoints. I like to change something in the code, re-run a d12 (or a d16 etc) and see if it helped, in an iteration loop. To see if a run helps, I like to monitor the wandb plots for: val_bpb (validation loss in vocab-size-invariant units of bits per byte) as a function of step , total_training_time and total_training_flops . core_metric (the DCLM CORE score) VRAM utilization, train/mfu (Model FLOPS utilization), train/tok_per_sec (training throughput) See an example here . The important thing to note is that nanochat is written and configured around one single dial of complexity - the depth of the transformer. This single integer automatically determines all other hyperparameters (the width of the transformer, number of heads, learning rate adjustments, training horizons, weight decays, ...) so that the trained model comes out compute optimal. The idea is that the user doesn't have to think about or set any of this, they are simply asking for a smaller or bigger model using --depth , and everything "just works". By sweeping out the depth, you achieve the nanochat miniseries of compute optimal models at various sizes. GPT-2 capability model (which is of most interest at the moment) happens to be somewhere around d24-d26 range with the current code. But any candidate changes to the repo have to be principled enough that they work for all settings of depth. Running on CPU / MPS The script runs/runcpu.sh shows a very simple example of running on CPU or Apple Silicon. It dramatically shrinks the LLM that is being trained to make things fit into a reasonable time interval of a few ten minutes of training. You will not get strong results in this way. Precision / dtype nanochat does not use torch.amp.autocast .

title: p-e-w/heretic
abstract:
Heretic Training-free language model modification Remove censorship , suppress slop, reduce sycophancy, and more. All in an afternoon, on your gaming PC. Modify any LLM that you can run on your hardware 1 Heretic is a unique tool that lets you do what only corporations with access
to massive computing power usually do: Modify, rather than merely run,
language models. It does not perform expensive training; rather, it uses
a collection of mathematical techniques to steer behavior based on contrasting
example prompts and matching scorers. Heretic can, depending on the configuration: Suppress refusals/remove censorship (this is the default action ) Reduce slop ( config.noslop.toml ) Reduce humor ( config.nohumor.toml ) Reduce sycophancy ( config.nosyco.toml ) Alter emotional alignment ( config.emotions.toml ) and many, many other things. ‼️ Using Heretic does NOT require understanding how language models work internally ‼️ In fact, you can go from zero to removing censorship from your first model in a matter of seconds . Heretic supports most dense models, including
many multimodal models, several different MoE architectures, and many modern
hybrid models. The community has created and published thousands of models with Heretic.
Heretic models have been independently benchmarked using standard metrics
like MMLU and GSM8K, and have been found to compare favorably against models
produced with competing abliteration tools. 2 3 Usage Prepare a Python 3.10+ environment with PyTorch 2.6+ installed as appropriate
for your hardware. Then run: pip install -U heretic-llm
heretic Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 Replace Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with whatever model you want to process. By default, Heretic performs censorship removal (refusal suppression). If you want to do something else, choose one of the configuration files linked
above, or write your own. See config.default.toml for available configuration options. Important Configuration files made for Heretic 1.x are not compatible with Heretic 2.x!
See the migration guide for what you need to change
in order to make your old configurations work. At the start of a program run, Heretic benchmarks the system to determine
the optimal batch size to make the most of the available hardware.
On an RTX 3090, with the default configuration, processing Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 takes about 30-40 minutes. After Heretic has finished processing a model, you are given the choice to
save the model, upload it to Hugging Face, chat with it to test how well it works,
run standard benchmarks on it, or any combination of those actions. Controlling what Heretic does using scorer plugins Heretic steers model behavior by optimizing one or multiple scores. Scores are
computed by scorer plugins. You can easily write your own scorers to get full
control over what Heretic does to models. The Scorer interface (abstract base class) your scorer needs to inherit from
is defined in scorer.py . The only required method
is get_score , but there is more machinery (such as settings management)
available when you need it. By default, Heretic scores models by refusal rate (implemented in keyword_rate.py ) and KL divergence
(implemented in kl_divergence.py ).
Additional scorers are available in the scorers directory .
These scorers can serve as examples for your own implementations, and can easily
be adapted to your needs. Scorers are configured through the main configuration file .
Which scorer plugins are active is determined by the scorers setting, which
also controls whether a scorer's score should be minimized or maximized during
optimization. Any number of scorers can be used simultaneously, and their scores
will be co-optimized. Multiple instances of the same scorer can be configured
with different settings. See the configuration file for the full documentation
of this mechanism. The path to a scorer plugin can be specified either as a fully qualified import
path ( fully.qualified.module.MyScorerClass ) or as a file path followed by
a class name ( path/to/plugin.py:MyScorerClass ). You do not have to modify
the Heretic package code in order to use your own plugins. Heretic also has modifier plugins, which are described in the next section . How Heretic works Heretic combines a pluggable modifier (interface in modifier.py ) with a TPE-based hyperparameter optimizer
powered by Optuna . The optimizer finds a set of parameters that,
when passed to the modifier, minimize or maximize a set of configurable scores on the resulting model ( see above ). Heretic ships with two modifiers: Arbitrary-Rank Ablation (ARA) 4 : This is the default modifier, and was
specifically developed for use in Heretic. You can find an overview of how ARA
works in the original pull request ,
and see the precise implementation in ara.py . Directional ablation aka "abliteration" 5 : The classic method for refusal
suppression. Heretic's implementation uses a flexible ablation weight kernel over
the layers, and supports both projected abliteration 6 and norm preservation (MPOA) 7 .
The complete code is in abliteration.py . You can use the modifiers setting to switch between modifier implementations.
Despite the name of the setting using a plural form, Heretic currently allows
only a single modifier for a given processing run. This may change in the future. Reproducibility and the Heretic Grimoire Heretic has the ability to create reproducible models whose repositories contain
all information required to produce a byte-for-byte identical model on demand,
provided that the environment is perfectly identical to the original one. PyTorch
doesn't guarantee that operations return identical outputs unless hardware, drivers,
operating system, and the entire software stack including all package versions
are exactly the same. Heretic manages all that complexity for you. When uploading a processed model to
Hugging Face, Heretic offers to include reproducibility information. This is entirely
optional, but if you choose to do so, the uploaded repository will contain a reproduce folder with detailed instructions for recreating the model
( example ).
This folder contains both human-readable instructions and a machine-readable manifest
file named reproduce.json , which includes all the information Heretic needs to automatically reproduce the model. Automatic reproduction can be performed with heretic --reproduce path/to/reproduce.json Heretic will guide you through the process, checking your environment against the one
that was used to create the model, and pointing out potentially problematic mismatches.
The multi-hour computations that were required to make the original model do not have to be re-done, and the entire process typically takes a few minutes. After you
have exported the resulting model, Heretic will verify the hashes of the weight files
against those stored in the reproduction manifest (they may or may not be identical,
depending on how closely your system resembles the original one). Many people have uploaded models with reproducibility information to Hugging Face.
Since a reproduction manifest is only around 9 kilobytes in size, these manifests
form a portable library of models that can be reproduced at will. That library is called the Heretic Grimoire. You can view it here . But you don't have to rely on an externally hosted web application to access the
library of manifests: The Grimoire is fundamentally designed as a distributed system,
and you can fetch your own local copies of publicly available manifests from
Hugging Face whenever you want by running heretic --collect-reproducibles path/to/target/folder/ You now have a local backup of all reproducible Heretic models, properly catalogued.
To update this collection, simply run the command again. It functions as an
append-only backup, never deleting files even if the corresponding model no longer
exists on Hugging Face. Heretic is made by humans!

title: koala73/worldmonitor
abstract:
World Monitor 簡體中文 | 日本語 | Русский Real-time global intelligence dashboard — AI-powered news aggregation, geopolitical monitoring, and infrastructure tracking in a unified situational awareness interface. Documentation · Releases · Contributing Ways to Use It Surface Get it Docs Web app worldmonitor.app and the tech, finance, commodity, happy and energy variants Getting Started Desktop app (Tauri) Windows, macOS and Linux downloads above Desktop App Terminal dashboard npx worldmonitor Terminal Dashboard CLI npm install -g worldmonitor or brew install worldmonitor Command-Line Client SDKs Python worldmonitor-sdk , Ruby worldmonitor , Go sdk/go SDKs MCP server https://worldmonitor.app/mcp MCP Overview The terminal dashboard runs the same live data in your shell: world map, news, markets, conflict, military flights, cyber, climate, prediction markets and live TV, with mouse support and colour themes. No API key needed. What It Does Curated news feeds across global and regional categories, AI-synthesized into briefs Dual map engine — 3D globe (globe.gl) and WebGL flat map (deck.gl) with a shared map-layer catalog Panel inventory — concrete panel implementations across specialized variants Cross-stream correlation — military, economic, disaster, and escalation signal convergence Country Instability Index (CII) — live CII v14 scores, bands, and approximate 24-hour movement for 31 Tier-1 countries Finance radar — stock exchanges, commodities, crypto, and a market composite Local AI — run everything with Ollama, no API keys required Site variants from a single codebase (world, tech, finance, commodity, happy, energy) Native desktop app (Tauri 2) for macOS, Windows, and Linux Multilingual UI with native-language feeds and RTL support For the full feature list, architecture, data sources, and algorithms, see the documentation . Support Status All site variants and desktop binaries are built from a single codebase and ship from the same release process. The table below clarifies maintenance status so you know which surfaces are safe to depend on. Surface Status Notes worldmonitor.app , tech. , finance. , commodity. , happy. , energy. Stable Public deployments built from this repo, actively maintained Desktop binaries (Windows / macOS Apple Silicon / macOS Intel / Linux AppImage) Stable One Tauri binary for every variant — install World Monitor and switch to tech, finance, commodity, energy, or happy in-app. There is deliberately no per-variant download worldmonitor npm package (terminal dashboard and CLI) Stable Published from cli/ on every cli-v* tag Issues filed against any of the above are triaged from the same backlog — see the issues board for currently-open work. Quick Start Requires Node.js 24, the version pinned in .nvmrc . Distribution packages are often older. Debian 12 and Raspberry Pi OS ship Node.js 18 with npm 9.2.0, where npm install stops with Invalid comparator: file:vendor/braces . Install Node.js 24 with nvm ( nvm install inside the checkout reads .nvmrc ) or from nodejs.org . git clone https://github.com/koala73/worldmonitor.git cd worldmonitor
npm install
npm run dev Open localhost:3000 (override the port with DEV_PORT in .env.local ). The app runs with no environment variables. Feature-specific data sources may require credentials. See .env.example for the full list. For variant-specific development: npm run dev:tech # tech.worldmonitor.app npm run dev:finance # finance.worldmonitor.app npm run dev:commodity # commodity.worldmonitor.app npm run dev:happy # happy.worldmonitor.app npm run dev:energy # energy.worldmonitor.app See the self-hosting guide for deployment options (Vercel, Docker, static). Tech Stack Category Technologies Frontend Vanilla TypeScript, Vite, globe.gl + Three.js, deck.gl + MapLibre GL Desktop Tauri 2 (Rust) with Node.js sidecar AI/ML Ollama / OpenRouter, Transformers.js (browser-side) API Contracts Protocol Buffers and sebuf HTTP annotations Deployment Vercel Edge Functions, Railway relay, Tauri, PWA Caching Redis (Upstash), 3-tier cache, CDN, service worker Full stack details in the architecture docs . Programmatic Access World Monitor is built for agents and scripts as well as browsers: MCP server — https://worldmonitor.app/mcp (Streamable HTTP). Public tools/list ; tools/call authenticates with a X-WorldMonitor-Key header or OAuth.
The server also publishes its Agent Skills through the draft io.modelcontextprotocol/skills extension ( skills/list , skills/get , and skill://… resource reads). Google Antigravity and Gemini listing preparation — install the bundled Antigravity plugin ( .antigravity-plugin/plugin.json + mcp_config.json ) with agy plugin install ./worldmonitor . Gemini custom apps and Connected Apps sign in through Google's OAuth callbacks. See Gemini and Antigravity . REST API — base https://api.worldmonitor.app , described by the OpenAPI spec . CLI — the official worldmonitor npm package (source in cli/ ). Run it with no arguments in a terminal for the terminal dashboard : npx worldmonitor tools # run ad-hoc — list every MCP tool (no key needed) npm install -g worldmonitor # or install the `worldmonitor` (alias `wm`) command brew install worldmonitor # or install it with Homebrew worldmonitor risk IR --api-key wm_xxx SDKs — official zero-dependency client libraries mirroring the CLI: Python worldmonitor-sdk (source in sdk/python/ ), Ruby worldmonitor ( sdk/ruby/ ), Go github.com/koala73/worldmonitor/sdk/go ( sdk/go/ ). Guide: worldmonitor.app/docs/sdks . Agent discovery files: llms.txt · agent-skills manifest · api-catalog . Get an API key at worldmonitor.app/pro . Flight Data Flight data provided graciously by Wingbits , the most advanced ADS-B flight data solution. Supported By World Monitor's web app and API run on Vercel . Thank you to Vercel for their generous support of the project. Data Sources WorldMonitor aggregates attributed upstream sources across geopolitics, finance, energy, climate, aviation, cyber, military, infrastructure, and news intelligence. Curated feeds and freshness-tracked source groups are published in the full data sources catalog , with provider, feed-tier, license-posture, and collection-method details. title: mvschwarz/openrig
abstract:
OpenRig A harness wraps a model. A rig wraps your harnesses. Define your agent team in YAML, boot it with one command. Claude Code and Codex in the same rig, managed as one system. OpenRig is open-source software for building and running your own network of agents. It turns AI coding agents from a pile of terminal sessions into a persistent, organized team. Talk to a lead agent about the outcome you want; it can coordinate specialists across teams and bring you results and decisions that need your attention. Start with a repository and one useful change, then keep the team's work and context at the same addresses. It's the open-source system behind my AI civilization experiments. Guide: Getting started · Stuck? Help · Questions: Q&A · Updates and demos: @_feralmachine on X See it running Start here: the guided first-use path : install, talk to the kernel operator, then choose a team for your first useful change. Not setting this up today? Get the next walkthrough and occasional OpenRig updates → https://openrig.dev/follow Install and first run Let your coding agent set it up. First check that node --version shows 22 or 24: the command below needs
Node.js and the npx that comes with it. Then, in your project folder, add OpenRig's rigs skill to the agent you
use: # Claude Code npx skills add https://github.com/mvschwarz/openrig/tree/v0.7.5/skills/rigs --skill rigs --agent claude-code # Codex npx skills add https://github.com/mvschwarz/openrig/tree/v0.7.5/skills/rigs --skill rigs --agent codex Then type /rigs in Claude Code, or $rigs in Codex, and say what you want built. The skill has your agent tell
you what it will run and change before it does, install OpenRig, open the OpenRig view and pass your goal to
OpenRig's operator. You need Node.js 22 or 24 (22 on Apple silicon), tmux, macOS or Linux (WSL2 on Windows), and Claude Code or Codex
signed in. One provider is enough to start. Already have OpenRig? Use the tag that matches rig --version , or upgrade first. Prefer to type the commands yourself? Install it yourself ↓ Requires Node.js 22 or 24 and tmux, on macOS or Linux, and one working Claude Code or Codex account: one is enough, since the kernel operator adapts the shipped starter team to whichever you have. On Linux, the distribution's own Node.js can be older (Ubuntu 24.04's is 18); install a supported version with nvm ( nvm install 22 ) or NodeSource. On a Mac with Apple silicon, use Node.js 22 ( compatibility history ). On a Mac where you aren't an administrator, or where Homebrew belongs to another account (its brew install is refused), install Node.js in your own home folder with nvm : run touch ~/.zshrc (a new Mac account has none, and nvm's installer only adds itself to a profile file that already exists), then nvm's install command, for nvm v0.40.8 curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.8/install.sh | bash ( nvm's page has the newest), open a new terminal, and run nvm install 22 . nvm itself needs no administrator password, and npm install -g then installs into your nvm folder. If nvm's installer says you need Apple's command line tools, run xcode-select --install , then its install command again. On Windows, use WSL2, the Windows route OpenRig supports; native Windows isn't supported. OpenRig's automated tests don't run on WSL2 yet; see one user's working setup . What OpenRig changes on your machine Install: @openrig/cli goes in globally with npm. Setup: rig setup adds an OpenRig block to ~/.tmux.conf . It can install tmux (with Homebrew on macOS), and
Herdr unless you pass --no-herdr . Plain rig setup , which is what the one-command install runs, checks both
Claude Code and Codex and may install a missing one; rig setup --providers claude (or codex ) limits it to
yours. Starting OpenRig, for the coding agent you use (paths are the usual defaults): Codex: hooks and trust in ~/.codex/config.toml . Claude Code: workspace trust in ~/.claude.json , and activity hooks in the project's .claude/settings.local.json , plus a status line unless you already have your own. Discovery skills go in ~/.claude/skills and ~/.agents/skills . Starting a team in your project: adds managed guidance to AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md , plus the team's skills
and plugins. Permissions: by default, OpenRig's own kernel gets broader permissions than a project team gets by default.
On Codex that's full access with no approval prompts ( -s danger-full-access -a never ). On Claude Code, its file
tools, web fetches and operational commands, including reads under your home folder, run without asking. A
permission policy, per-agent choice or Codex profile changes that. What your team can do depends on the team you
choose and your settings; workshop , for example, ships with broad access. Backups: OpenRig doesn't guarantee it can preserve or roll back these files, so back them up first. Everything OpenRig writes, and why → Install it yourself This runs OpenRig's install script from the v0.7.5 release. It checks Node.js and npm, installs the latest published @openrig/cli with npm install -g , runs the Node.js and SQLite check, then runs rig setup --dry-run and rig setup . The first line prints that plan and changes nothing: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mvschwarz/openrig/v0.7.5/scripts/install.sh | sh -s -- --dry-run
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mvschwarz/openrig/v0.7.5/scripts/install.sh | sh If a provider isn't signed in yet, the last step reports FAILED [4/4] , and rig setup lists the sign-in under "Some steps need attention". If the only remaining failures are provider sign-ins, the install steps finished; sign in to each selected provider as below and continue. Or step by step: npm install -g @openrig/cli
rig setup --dry-run To install with Bun instead, run bun add -g @openrig/cli . OpenRig still runs on Node.js, so install Node.js 22 as well. Bun may block this package's postinstall script, in which case the Node.js and SQLite check described under what OpenRig changes on your machine does not run at install time. npm 11 and later can skip that postinstall script and print npm warn install-scripts naming @openrig/cli . That's expected: the CLI still works, and only the Node.js and SQLite check was skipped. To run it yourself, use node "$(npm root -g)/@openrig/cli/scripts/check-abi.mjs" ; rig doctor checks the Node.js version only. Choose the working account you already have: Claude Code, Codex, or both . Reuse an explicit choice; no second subscription is required. rig setup --dry-run previews the broader setup; applying rig setup checks both harnesses and installs a missing one, plus Herdr unless declined with --no-herdr . Pass the choice with --providers claude or --providers codex so the other reads not selected instead of failed. The one-command install above doesn't know the choice, so it installs and checks both; for one provider, go step by step and run rig setup --providers <choice> . On macOS, the installing agent offers Ghostty once. Setup leaves an existing cmux installation alone. It is optional for the selected-provider path . A team seat with no permission policy, per-seat choice or (for Codex) named profile launches with OpenRig's team default : Claude runs ordinary rig commands, project reads and common tests without prompting, while lifecycle commands such as rig up and rig down still ask; Codex also gets the OpenRig workspace and its pod's state directory as writable directories. Before launching, your agent recommends keeping that default, and offers to remember selected OpenRig commands in your native settings only if you want that, at personal project scope unless you explicitly choose user-wide sessions. It is not global YOLO or permission to invent work. On Yes, the agent adds and verifies native rules ; No or no answer keeps the team default and leaves settings unchanged. An existing explicit choice is reused.

title: cheaper-inference/OmniRoute
abstract:
🚀 OmniRoute — The Free AI Gateway 💰 ~1.62B Tokens / Month Across Third-Party Free Tiers Bring your own provider accounts. This is an estimated aggregate across separately eligible third-party free tiers, not a token grant from OmniRoute. Sign up, obtain credentials where required, and connect the providers you can use; each provider controls its limits, availability, and terms. Stacking free tiers by hand is painful — dozens of SDKs, dozens of rate limits, and no idea how much you actually have. OmniRoute catalogs 485 free-tier entries across 34 recurring pool keys and computes the token headline from the 17 pools with a published positive monthly budget plus five per-model Groq caps , deduplicated by shared pool. Quotas that only open after a regional identity check (today: ModelScope) are shown apart, +~6M behind regional identity verification, and never summed into the headline. The result stays visible on the dashboard ( /dashboard/free-tiers ). Animated summary of the live /dashboard/free-tiers page. Full methodology (pool dedupe, credit tiers, provider terms): docs/reference/FREE_TIERS.md . These figures are re-audited every two weeks against the live catalog and move both ways — a provider ends a free tier and the number drops; a new one lands and it climbs. We publish what the catalog actually computes, never a rounded-up best case. ⭐ Star the repo if OMNIROUTE helped you save money and make your work easier. 💬 Join the community 👋 Follow the maintainer — get new providers, releases & tips first: Questions, provider tips, roadmap & support → Discord · Telegram · WhatsApp 🌍 Global / 🇧🇷 Brasil / Portal 📈 The Gateway Keeps Growing v3.8.50 v3.8.51 v3.8.53+ 🌐 Providers 352 358 380 🧠 Unique chat model IDs 1320 1374 1475 🖼️ Modality Bridge 🆕 vision + audio + video ✓ ✓ 📡 Radar free catalog 🆕 opt-in ✓ ✓ ⚖️ Quota-aware scheduling 🆕 Quota-Share ✓ ✓ 📊 Quota telemetry 🆕 live ✓ ✓ 🧰 Headless mode — — 🆕 serve --headless 🛤️ LTS rail infra — — 🆕 release channels 🔎 Model discovery API — — 🆕 /v1/models/query → Roadmap — riding the rail to v3.9.0 LTS 🧩 Available 🚀 Start 🚀 Quick Start 📦 Install 🆓 Connect a provider 💡 Learn 💥 The Promise 🤔 Why OmniRoute 🏆 What Sets Apart ⚙️ Features 🎯 Combos 🌐 Providers 🔌 CLI & MCP 🗜️ Compression 🖥️ Where It Runs 🔒 Private 👀 See it 🎬 In Action ✨ What's New 🤖 Compatible CLIs 💚 Support 💚 Support / Donate 💬 Community 💖 Sponsors 📦 Project 🛠️ Tech Stack 📖 Docs 👥 Contributors 🌐 In 67 languages 🆓 Install, connect a provider, then route through one endpoint # After connecting a provider, copy your OmniRoute key from Dashboard → Endpoints: curl http://localhost:20128/v1/chat/completions \
  -H " Authorization: Bearer YOUR_OMNIROUTE_KEY " \
  -H " Content-Type: application/json " \
  -d ' {"model":"auto","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello!"}]} ' auto needs an eligible route. A fresh installation can have no eligible keyless targets, and a keyless provider may reject third-party clients. Providers marked tos: avoid , including Kiro, are excluded from automatic routing by default; connecting an account does not override that setting. See the Free Tiers Guide before choosing a provider. 📦 Copy-paste quickstart scripts for Python, Node.js, PHP, and cURL → examples/quickstart/ 💥 The Promise 🤔 Why OmniRoute? 🤝 Supported by our Open Source Friends Want to join as an Open Source Friend? These are the companies that back open source and help keep OmniRoute moving — and we say publicly where every token they give us goes. Reach out: diegosouza.pw@outlook.com Kimi Moonshot AI Thanks to Kimi (Moonshot AI) , our founding Open Source Friend, for backing this project! Kimi is the AI lab behind the open-weight K2 and K3 model families — Kimi K3 delivers a 1M-token context window, native vision and frontier-level coding at a fraction of closed-model prices, and works out of the box with Claude Code, Codex and every coding tool OmniRoute serves. What Kimi's support powers: Kimi's API credits power OmniRoute's AI-validated release pipeline — the merge validation powered by Kimi K3 stage that reviews every pull request before it ships — plus day-to-day feature development. First-class Kimi support ships on both rails: the direct Kimi API ( kimi-k3 ) and the Kimi Code coding plan (OAuth and API key). OmniRoute is also the first Brazilian open-source project in Kimi's support program. Get a Kimi API key with 15% extra credits → Cheaper Inference cheaperinference.com Thanks to Cheaper Inference , an OmniRoute Open Source Friend, for backing this project! Cheaper Inference is a cost-ranked gateway that resells 42 frontier models — Claude, GPT-5.x, Gemini, Kimi K3, GLM, DeepSeek, Grok and MiniMax — behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, routing each request to the cheapest eligible provider without ever charging above the model maker's list price. First-class support in OmniRoute: Chat Completions, the native /v1/responses endpoint, vision, tool calling and 3 image models ( grok-imagine , nano-banana-pro , nano-banana-2 , reachable as cheaperinference/<model> ). Available models include claude-opus-4-8 , claude-opus-5 , gpt-5.6-sol and more. Grab your $100 → ⚠️ Affiliate link — OmniRoute has no sponsorship or partnership with this provider. title: mksglu/context-mode
hieunc229/mailflare
abstract:
Mailflare A self-hosted alternative to Google Workspace. Setup custom domain Emails , Calendar, Drive, Booking and built-in AI agents . Run it on Cloudflare or Docker. Send and receive with Cloudflare, Resend or Amazon SES. Store files in R2, Backblaze B2 or AWS S3. Use D1, Postgres, MySQL or Turso for the database. Screenshots Inbox Domains Mailboxes Calendar Booking Drive Sponsors Want to support Mailflare? Become a sponsor . Features Apps Email : Custom domain mailboxes, personal or shared, with access you control. Send and receive with Cloudflare Email, Resend or Amazon SES. Routing rules : Store, forward, reject or sort incoming mail. Calendar : Repeating events with time zones. Attendees get email invitations. Booking : Share a public link so anyone can book a free time on your calendar. Drive : Store and share files. AI agents : Search mail, draft replies and manage events. Connect other AI tools over MCP. Technical Databases : Cloudflare D1 (default), PostgreSQL, MySQL, Turso / libSQL, or a local SQLite file. Set DATABASE_URL to switch. Works with Supabase, Neon, PlanetScale, TiDB and more. See Databases . File storage : Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2 or AWS S3. Hosting : Cloudflare Workers or a single Docker container. Admin : Users, API keys, webhooks, audit logs and backups. Import : Bring in mail from IMAP, Gmail Takeout, .eml and .mbox files. Mailflare currently supports 34 languages, including English, Português (Brasil), Português (Portugal), Español, Français, Deutsch, Italiano, Nederlands, Polski, Українська, Русский, Türkçe, 中文（簡體）, 日本語, 한국어, Bahasa Indonesia, Bahasa Melayu, Tiếng Việt, ไทย, हिन्दी, বাংলা, मराठी, తెలుగు, தமிழ், ગુજરાતી, ಕನ್ನಡ, മലയാളം, ਪੰਜਾਬੀ, සිංහල, Kiswahili, Hausa, plus العربية, اردو and فارسی (right-to-left). Cost You can receive and send mail for free. Receiving : Cloudflare Email Routing is free. Sending : Use the free tier of Resend (3,000 emails a month) or Amazon SES. Cloudflare's own sending needs the $5/month Paid Worker plan. New Amazon SES accounts start in a sandbox. Ask AWS for production access to lift it. Prices change, so check Resend , Amazon SES and Cloudflare . Deploy Deploy the app. Click Deploy to Cloudflare . Keep the app name mailflare , or it will break. Finish setup. Open the app at /setup and create your admin account. Connect a domain. Add a domain from the same Cloudflare account, then create your first mailbox. CF_TOKEN is required. Create a scoped Cloudflare API token with these permissions: All accounts: Email Sending:Edit, DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Addresses:Edit All zones: DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Rules:Edit, Zone Settings:Edit, DNS:Edit More options: deployment guide . Deploy with an AI agent Paste this into an AI agent that has terminal access (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and similar): Install Mailflare for me from https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare on my Cloudflare account.

1. Read README.md, docs/deployment.md and wrangler.jsonc first.
2. Ask me for my Cloudflare account ID and two API tokens, using a secret input:
   a deploy token (for Wrangler) and a runtime token (the Worker secret CF_TOKEN).
   Never print them, commit them, or pass them as command arguments.
3. Keep the Worker name exactly "mailflare". Create or reuse the D1 database
   "mailflare", the R2 bucket "mailflare-raw", and the queues "mailflare-inbound",
   "mailflare-outbound" and "mailflare-agent".
4. Install dependencies, run `npm run deploy`, and set CF_TOKEN as a Worker secret.
   Do not run remote database migrations yourself. The /setup page does that.
5. Give me the app URL and anything I still need to do. I will open /setup, create
   the admin account and connect my domain. Token permissions and more options: deployment guide . Self-host with Docker Runs as one container on any server, with SQLite and local files. cp .env.docker.example .env.docker
docker compose up -d --build See self-hosting . Local development cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars
npm install
npm run db:migrate:local
npm run dev Add your Cloudflare credentials to .dev.vars , then open localhost:3000 . Run npm run db:seed to load sample data. npm run build : build the Worker npm run deploy : build and deploy npm run lint : lint and type check A schema change needs a migration for each database type. See Databases . Documentation Deployment and configuration Databases Sending and receiving providers API and integrations Email assistant and MCP Adding a language Troubleshooting License See LICENSE .

title: vercel-labs/skills
abstract:
skills The CLI for the open agent skills ecosystem. Agent skills are reusable instructions that teach coding agents how to perform tasks,
from reviewing code to working with a library. Discover skills at skills.sh . Supports OpenCode , Claude Code , Codex , Cursor , and 75 more . Install a Skill Requires Node.js 22.20 or later. Run this from your project: npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills Choose the skills and coding agents to install to. Skills are installed to the current
project by default; add -g to make them available across projects. # Choose one skill and agent npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-skills --skill web-design-guidelines -a claude-code # Browse available skills npx skills find See the installation reference for source formats,
private repositories, and all options. Other Commands Command Description npx skills find [query] Search for skills npx skills list List installed skills npx skills use <source>@<skill> Use one skill without installing npx skills check Check for available updates npx skills update [skills...] Update installed skills npx skills remove [skills...] Remove installed skills npx skills init [name] Create a skill template Read the CLI reference or run npx skills --help for examples and options. Experimental commands are listed below . Use a Skill Without Installing Generate a prompt for a skill, or launch a supported coding agent with it: npx skills use vercel-labs/agent-skills@web-design-guidelines --agent claude-code Omit --agent to print the prompt instead. See skills use . Experimental Features Commands prefixed with experimental_ are previews. Their names, options, and behavior may change or be removed in any release without notice. Command Description npx skills experimental_sync Sync skills shipped by npm dependencies into your project npx skills experimental_install Restore project skills recorded in skills-lock.json Some npm packages bundle instructions for your agent alongside their code. Sync links them into your project so they update with the dependency, and also installs skill packs declared in package.json : npm install -D skills agent-browser
npx skills experimental_sync -y See the experimental commands reference for options, the skills field, and the RFC behind it. Supported Agents The CLI detects installed agents and lets you choose where skills are installed.
See all supported agents, installation paths, and compatibility . Creating Skills npx skills init my-skill Edit the generated SKILL.md with instructions for your agent.
See creating and sharing skills for the format and discovery rules. Documentation CLI reference : installation, command examples, and experimental features Supported agents : agent names, skill directories, and compatibility Creating skills : frontmatter, repository layouts, and plugins Troubleshooting and configuration : common problems, environment variables, and telemetry Telemetry The CLI collects anonymous usage data. Set DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 or DO_NOT_TRACK=1 to disable telemetry and security-audit requests.
See what is collected . Related Links Skills Directory Agent Skills Specification Vercel Agent Skills License This project is licensed under the MIT License .

title: kgoedecke/doop
abstract:
Doop is the open-source alternative to Paper.design — a multiplayer
design canvas for humans and AI agents. Every design lives on a shareable Canvas ( /c/<id> ) holding Frames — artboards that render real HTML in sandboxed iframes. People edit
in the browser; AI agents edit through the built-in MCP server , streaming their designs in
live. Everyone sees everything as it happens: cursors, presence, frame edits, agent status, and an
activity feed. Think of it as Claude Design for whichever agent you already use: Claude Code, Codex, ChatGPT,
Cursor, OpenCode or any other MCP client designs on the same canvas, and the built-in Doop Agent
runs on GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi or Qwen models
( every agent and model ). Design with agents, not prompts-and-refresh — connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) once,
then watch it sketch, stream and self-review designs on your canvas, next to your cursor. A built-in Doop Agent — queue a card or @mention a role and it designs on its own, no client
to connect. Runs on the model account each user connects (a ChatGPT subscription , or an
OpenAI, Claude, Gemini or OpenRouter key), or on the server's ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for as many
free tasks as RESIDENT_TASK_LIMIT grants (none by default) ( setup ); the
first-canvas welcome performance is scripted and runs without any of it. Pages within a canvas — organize frames into named pages from the Layers panel. Add, rename,
drag to reorder, double-click to rename, or right-click to rename and delete empty pages.
Page edits support Undo/Redo; selected frames can move between pages. Agents can list pages
with get_canvas , manage them with set_canvas_pages (passing the original list as expectedPages to protect collaborators), and target frames with pageId . Clickable prototypes — wire elements to other frames (click, hover, press, key or delay;
navigate, overlay, back, scroll or link, with transitions) in Prototype mode or straight in the
HTML, then click through the flow with Play or share /c/<id>/proto . Agents use the same data-doop-* attributes plus get_prototype / set_prototype_start . A real canvas editor — draw frames, shapes, pen paths and text, edit any element's fill,
type and flex layout, snap to rulers and guides, zoom from 8% to 1600%
( the editor ). True multiplayer — live cursors, presence, follow mode, per-frame editing indicators,
undo/redo, threaded comments on elements or the canvas, and an activity feed, all over one
WebSocket room. Design memory — pin exemplar frames, capture decisions, and let the distiller propose durable
style rules that every agent follows. Private by default — invite collaborators by email or share a link that can view, comment
or edit; agents inherit exactly their human's access. Self-host in one command — docker compose up , or bun run dev with zero configuration
(embedded Postgres, no external services required). Works with any agent Doop isn't tied to one model vendor. Every agent below designs through the same MCP server, works
as the person who connected it, and shows up live on the canvas with its own cursor, status and
tasks. Connect AI in the top bar walks you through each one. Agent How it connects Claude Code claude mcp add , OAuth in the browser ( setup ) Claude (web and desktop) Add to Claude in Connect AI ( setup ) Codex (CLI and desktop) codex mcp add , OAuth in the browser ( setup ) ChatGPT A custom MCP server in ChatGPT, guided by Connect AI → ChatGPT Cursor Add to Cursor in Connect AI OpenCode, VS Code Copilot, OpenClaw and more Any MCP client, over OAuth or with an agent key ( setup ) Headless agents (n8n, Mastra, CI) An agent key as a bearer header ( setup ) No agent of your own? The built-in Doop Agent runs on the model account you
connect: a ChatGPT subscription, or an OpenAI, Claude, Gemini or OpenRouter key. OpenRouter brings
DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, GLM and MiniMax ( details ). Quickstart git clone https://github.com/kgoedecke/doop && cd doop
bun install
bun run dev Doop builds and installs with bun ( bun.lock is the only
lockfile); the server itself runs on Node. Web app: http://localhost:4300 API + WebSocket + MCP server: http://localhost:4400 (the web port proxies /api , /ws , /mcp , /.well-known , /i/ , /ingest and /local-agent to it) bun run dev and bun run build also package the Claude Desktop extension with a Node script,
so Node must be on your PATH as well. Everything works with no configuration: data persists to an embedded Postgres (PGlite) in data/pg ,
and every optional integration (SMTP, stock photos, object storage, analytics) degrades gracefully
until its variable in .env.example is set ( the ones that matter ).
The built-in Doop Agent runs once a user connects a model account in Settings
(or on the server's ANTHROPIC_API_KEY if you raise RESIDENT_TASK_LIMIT ) — agents you connect
yourself over MCP need no key. Or self-host the production build with Docker: BETTER_AUTH_SECRET= $( openssl rand -hex 32 ) docker compose up -d # app + Postgres on :4400 Production build without Docker: bun run build && bun run start (single server on :4400 serving
everything). Set DATABASE_URL to use a real Postgres — same code path as PGlite. Prefer not to run anything? doop.design is the hosted version. Once you sign in, Home is where you start: describe what you want and Doop makes a canvas with
drafts queued for the Doop Agent, or pick up one of your canvases, workspaces and connected agents. The canvas editor The bottom toolbar holds the tools; every one has a single-key shortcut. Shapes drawn on the
canvas become standalone elements, and shapes drawn inside a frame become positioned HTML/SVG
layers of that frame, so agents read and edit them like any other markup. Tool Key What it does Select V Click to select, drag the background for a marquee, ⇧/⌘-click to add to the selection Hand H Pan (Space or the middle button pans from any tool) Frame F Draw an empty frame Rectangle R Draw a rectangle Circle O Draw a circle or ellipse Vector path P Bézier pen: snaps to its own anchors, previews closing the path; Alt skips snapping Text T Place a text layer Comment C Pin a comment to an element or to the canvas Frames — drag to move, pull the corner handle to resize, snap to neighbours and guides.
The Inspector edits name,
position, size and the raw HTML, marks the frame ready for dev, exports it, and pins it as a
style reference; Version history… in the frame menu previews and restores earlier designs. Elements inside a frame — click to select, drag a corner grip or edge to resize (⇧ keeps the
ratio; a W × H badge shows the size), drag the element to
move it within or across frames. The Design tab edits fill, stroke, text (font, size, weight,
alignment), opacity, corner radius, rotation, position, flex layout (direction, gap, padding,
wrap, alignment) and image fills; HTML shows its source; Prototype wires interactions. The
floating toolbar adds Comment, Ask AI (pre-fills an @mention ), Code, Edit text and Copy link. Path editing — double-click a path to drag its anchors and Bézier handles, switch points
between corner and curve, or delete them. Alt moves one handle on its own; ⇧ constrains its angle. Layers — a searchable tree of pages, frames and elements: drag to reorder or reparent, hide,
lock, collapse, and right-click an element for copy, paste, duplicate, Copy HTML, Copy selector
and Copy link to element. Rulers and guides — ⇧R shows rulers; drag out of one to add a guide. Guides belong to the page,
undo like any edit, and everything snaps to them within 8 screen pixels. Zoom — 8% to 1600%. Wheel pans, ⌘/Ctrl + wheel or a pinch zooms; a 1px pixel grid fades in from
300%. The zoom menu has 50/100/200% presets and the rulers toggle. Panels — the right side panel has Agents , Comments , Activity and Memory tabs;
Layers and the side panel can be resized, and ⌘. hides all UI. Themes — Light, Dark or System under Settings → Appearance.
