abstract: CalibRaw A free, open-source RAW photo editor for Linux, Android, Windows and macOS, with a complete photo-development workflow and AI tools that run locally. Download • Why CalibRaw • Features • FAQ • Supported Formats • Building Website • Discord • Instagram Library AI Masks Effects Android Edit RAW files with sliders, curves, color grading and masks. AI tools can select a subject or the sky, remove objects and denoise high-ISO photos. Everything runs on your device , without an account or subscription. Download Platform Get it Linux (x86_64 / ARM64) Flathub , or .AppImage or .deb (Debian 13+, Ubuntu 24.04+) from the latest release Android (ARM64) F-Droid , or .apk from the latest release Windows (x86_64 / ARM64) Installer or portable .zip from the latest release macOS (Apple Silicon / Intel) .zip from the latest release AI models are downloaded once, on first use and only after you agree; they are verified by SHA-256 and then run offline. Graphics requirements CalibRaw processes photos on the GPU through Vulkan, Direct3D 12 or Metal. OpenGL is not supported: a GPU whose only driver is OpenGL cannot be used, and CalibRaw shows an "Unsupported graphics driver" notice instead of the editor. Platform Needs Linux A Vulkan driver. GPUs without one (for example Intel Haswell, whose Mesa Vulkan driver hasvk is not conformant and hidden) can run on the CPU with Mesa's software driver lavapipe ( mesa-vulkan-drivers or vulkan-swrast ), which is slow. Android A Vulkan-capable GPU and driver. Windows Direct3D 12 or Vulkan. Without either, Windows' software renderer (WARP) is used. macOS Metal. Set WGPU_BACKEND (for example vulkan ) to choose the graphics API yourself. Why CalibRaw Photo-development controls: Light, Tone Curve, Color, Color Mixer, Color Grading, Detail, Optics, Effects and Masks panels, with a scene-referred pipeline, Sigmoid tone mapping and highlight recovery. Offline AI: Subject, sky, depth and click-to-select object masks, AI Remove (Big-LaMa) that blends its fill into your photo's grain, and RawNIND denoise for Bayer and X-Trans RAWs. Native interface and GPU processing: Written in Rust with wgpu , WGSL compute shaders and an egui interface. Android support: The Android app uses the same engine and .calibraw sidecars as the desktop app, with layouts for touch controls. Broad camera support: Opens RAW files supported by LibRaw and Rawler, covering a wide range of camera makers and models; see the linked support lists below. Fast library browsing: Generates proxy-based previews and caches thumbnails and display metadata for quicker browsing. Library organization: Filter photos by rating and pick/reject flags, and sort by file modification date, filename, file size, rating or flag. Effects with masks: Apply depth-based fog, rain and relighting, wet surfaces with puddles and reflections, smoke, light rays, glow, halation, edge glow, neon and lens, motion, radial or tilt-shift blur to the whole photo or inside a mask. Edit Replay: Export a 30 FPS MP4 showing your edit step by step for Reels, Shorts or before/after posts. Key Features Rust & GPU Compute: Built with egui and wgpu , with compute shaders for image processing. Color Grading & Point Color: Sample colors directly with an eyedropper, fine-tune custom Hue, Saturation, and Luminance ranges, and preview affected areas with a live selection mask. Demosaicing: Shader-based Bayer RCD, Fujifilm X-Trans (Markesteijn 3-pass), and Dual Demosaicing to reduce noise and artifacts in high-ISO images. Sigmoid Tone Mapping: Smooth highlight roll-off inspired by modern scene-referred color workflows, paired with Opposed and LCh highlight recovery. Local AI Tools (Offline): Subject, sky, depth and object masks, AI Denoise, and AI Remove. Android App: An ARM64 NDK build with 16 KB memory page support, touch layouts, and MediaStore exporting. Non-Destructive Edits: All sliders, curves, and masks are saved to lightweight .calibraw JSON sidecar files. Presets: Save any combination of adjustment groups, masks and profile choices as a named preset, apply it in Develop or to a whole Library selection, and share it as a .calibraw-preset file. Imported .xmp presets stay as their source, so unsupported settings are kept for later versions; their tone curves, Point Color, lens corrections and Subject, Background, Sky, gradient and luminance-range masks are translated on load. LUTs: Import .cube 3D LUTs and apply one per photo with an Amount slider. Batch exports can apply a preset and a LUT to every photo without changing their edits. Tiled Export & CLI: Exports large RAW files in tiles to avoid GPU memory limits, plus a command-line tool for batch rendering. JPEG XL Export: Exports lossless .jxl images at 8-bit or 16-bit precision, including EXIF metadata when enabled. Edit Replay: Export a short 30 FPS MP4 that replays the current edit by category. Tooling & Workflow Color & Tone Point Color: Sample a color in global or mask HSL controls, refine its Hue/Saturation/Luminance span, preview the selected range, and apply targeted shifts. 8-Band Color Mixer: Adjust Hue, Saturation, and Luminance across 8 individual color bands. 3-Way Color Grading: Dedicated Shadows, Midtones, Highlights, and Global color wheels mapped through Oklab color space. Tone Curves: Luminance curve and individual Red, Green, and Blue splines with monotonic limits. Sigmoid Tone Mapping: Provides smooth, film-like highlight compression without harsh clipping. Demosaicing & Corrections Bayer RCD: Directional interpolation for standard Bayer sensors. Fujifilm X-Trans: Directional derivative and homogeneity demarcation pipeline for Fuji sensors. Dual Demosaicing: Blends edge-preserving and smoothed passes to suppress chroma noise at high ISOs. Automatic Lens Correction: Matches available camera and lens profiles through Lensfun and can automatically correct distortion, chromatic aberration and vignetting. Chromatic Aberration Removal: Works with any lens, profiled or not. Measures how far red and blue sit from green across the frame and moves them back into place, then removes the purple, blue and green fringes that remain along high-contrast edges. HDR Merge: Combine multiple bracketed RAW exposures into one extended-range image. Focus Stacking: Combine RAW frames focused at different distances into one image that is sharp throughout. Masking & AI Masks: Brush, Linear Gradient, Radial Gradient, and Shape masks with independent curves and adjustments. AI Masks: Subject and background (BiRefNet), sky (SkySeg U2Net), depth range (experimental; Depth Anything V2), click-to-select objects (SAM 2.1), and people with their face, skin, hair, clothes, lips, teeth or glasses on desktop (RF-DETR-Seg and Sapiens2, with BiRefNet outlines at High quality). AI Remove: Big-LaMa fills removed objects at native resolution where possible and restores the photo's own grain around the fill. Clone & Heal: Classic retouching brushes with aligned, fixed and registered source modes. AI Denoise: RawNIND denoises Bayer RAWs while demosaicing them and X-Trans RAWs in linear RGB. Privacy: Every model runs on your device. Models are downloaded only after you agree, and verified by SHA-256. Creative Effects Apply effects to the whole photo or stack them on a local mask. The Effects card adds Glow, Halation, Grain and Vignette in one click; every effect is in the Add menu. Each card keeps its main controls visible, with optional details collapsed. Hide a card to compare, reset its settings, or remove it independently. While their card is open, Relight, Light Rays, Radial Blur, Tilt-Shift and Vignette also show controls on the photo: drag a light or center into place, and rotate or widen the Tilt-Shift focus band directly. Blur & Movement: Soften distractions with Blur, shape bokeh with Lens Blur, add directional trails with Motion Blur, zoom or spin with Radial Blur, or keep a band in focus with Tilt Shift. Feather the mask for a smooth transition.

title: AI delivers 'zero financial payoff' to most companies, Apollo economist says
abstract:
AI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to a note recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch). Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said. Is this simply a matter of non-tech companies lagging behind the tech giants? Slok sounded skeptical, arguing that it will be tough for corporate America to “turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins.” “AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote, later adding, “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.” Recent studies have also found that AI has yet to deliver significant productivity gains .

title: It wasn't AI that flipped Proton's charge
abstract:
I’ve been paying for Proton for many years, and it’s what I recommend when someone asks how to get off Gmail. This week 404 Media published an investigation into how Proton’s leadership is pushing AI inside the company. The detail that made the rounds came from the security Slack channel: an engineer asked for a few days to pentest new code before shipping it, and CEO Andy Yen answered that it was “bullshit and loser thinking” , then told the team to stop lovingly handcrafting code and use AI more. For the first time, I’m not sure I’d still recommend them. A lot of the reactions treat this as an AI story, as if any AI-written code poisons the well, and I think that misses the point. Engineers using AI to write code is the new norm. It’s fine as long as there are guardrails around it: someone reviews what the model produced, it gets tested, and someone is accountable for what ships . What the reporting describes is a CEO telling an engineer, in front of colleagues, that raising a security concern was “loser thinking” . Staff were told their AI usage could decide whether they kept their jobs , and when that plan was dropped after it leaked, Yen said it had already served its purpose . None of this is about AI. Plenty of companies are rolling out coding agents right now without humiliating anyone, so if Proton can’t, the problem sits with its leadership. The tradeoff Proton can’t make For most companies, trading some caution for speed is a reasonable call. Proton is a privacy company, though, and what its users pay for is the confidence that the people building it are careful. Shipping slowly and carefully is part of what they’re selling. A bad release from a B2B vendor can be catastrophic , but for a company like Proton, a bug that exposes users’ mail would be fatal. One of the employees defending the company on Reddit added some context that was meant to help: Yen was fine with pentesting, as long as it didn’t slow down the pipeline. This is one of a few employees pretending to courageously dissent, but in reality agreeing with the official corporate line. It reads like astroturfing and a clumsy attempt at crisis management. No employee who shared on Reddit disagrees with how things were handled or with where the company is going. Beyond the clumsiness, it shows a leadership that now treats the constraints that made Proton worth paying for as the thing slowing it down. I’d like to keep recommending Proton, but that depends on the engineer asking for a few more days of testing still winning the argument against a leadership obsessed with velocity and arbitrary release dates.

title: China's First Frontier AI Export Controls: Mofcom Announcement No. 48
abstract:
Authors: Cloud Security Alliance AI Safety Initiative Published: 2026-10-23 Categories: AI Governance and Regulation Download PDF Download Markdown China’s First Frontier AI Export Controls: MOFCOM Announcement No. 48 Key Takeaways On October 16, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) issued Announcement No. 48 of 2026. The announcement proposes adding 40 technologies to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export , 23 of them in artificial intelligence, and it imposes an interim pre-export registration requirement that is already in effect [1][2]. China’s catalogue has touched AI before: the 2020 revision added personalized recommendation and AI interaction interface technology [6]. Unlike those 2020 additions, the draft reaches frontier model weights, agent architectures, and AI-enabled offensive cyber capability, with explicit technical thresholds for each [1]. The announcement contains two instruments with different legal status. The catalogue additions are a draft open for comment until November 15, 2026, while the registration requirement applies now, including to exports that have started but are not yet complete [1][2]. Within the draft, model weights are restricted at frontier scale. Weights, key checkpoints, source code, architecture, and training and inference optimization know-how are restricted if a model meets any one of three tests: at least 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, at least 2 trillion parameters, or a global top-10 position on public evaluation rankings, global call volume, or comparable measures at the time of export [1][3]. Agents are controlled independently of the model. Planning, multi-agent coordination, tool use, and game-theoretic decision technologies are restricted above set benchmarks, and high-performance agents built for critical infrastructure, defense, or core government use are prohibited outright [1]. The line between service access and custody determines most enterprise exposure. MOFCOM says API, app, web, SaaS, and lightweight on-device use do not count as exporting a large model. Deploying a restricted model locally outside China does count, though automatic licensing may apply on a Chinese company’s own overseas cloud [2]. Multinationals also face exposure through licensing deals and changes of ownership or control, not only through product exports, and analysts read the registration form as potentially capturing intra-group code sharing as well [2][3][4]. Any transfer of ownership, licensing for overseas use, or shift of control to a foreign entity can trigger registration [2][4]. Background China regulates outbound technology transfer under two overlapping regimes. The first is the technology-trade regime under the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, which governs the catalogue being revised here. The second is the dual-use export-control regime under the 2020 Export Control Law [5]. MOFCOM’s spokesperson described the revision as routine and grounded in Article 20 of the Foreign Trade Law. The spokesperson stressed that it “does not target any specific country, region, or entity” and that the aim is to prevent uncontrolled diffusion while protecting legitimate cooperation [2]. The catalogue has been revised several times since 2001. The August 2020 revision, which added recommendation-algorithm technology, coincided with the proposed sale of TikTok to a U.S. buyer and was reported as likely to complicate that deal [3][6]. Across all three sectors, Announcement No. 48 proposes 14 prohibited and 26 restricted items: 23 in AI, 5 in biomedicine, and 12 in photovoltaics [2]. In China’s technology-trade framework, prohibited technologies may not be exported at all, while restricted technologies require a license from commerce and science authorities. ChinaTalk notes that licensing is administered by provincial authorities, although central authorities have intervened in prominent cases [3]. The official annex groups the AI items into large models, agents, compute clusters, chip design, and information-processing technologies. It also excludes from management any technology that has already entered the public domain through open-source release or academic publication [1]. The interim registration requirement is the part that applies today. From the announcement date until the revised catalogue takes effect, exporters must register through MOFCOM’s unified business platform before exporting any listed technology. Registration covers four triggers: transfer of technology ownership abroad, licensing of domestic technology for overseas use, a change in ownership or control that makes a foreign entity the owner or controller, and other cases MOFCOM designates [2][4]. Exporters must decide for themselves whether a technology falls within scope. The registration form asks for recipient details, destination, technology description, end use, and estimated value [2][4]. The timing also matters for enterprises that already track U.S. controls. CSA’s prior research documented the first U.S. use of export-control authority to suspend a broadly deployed commercial frontier model [9]. Announcement No. 48 means frontier AI supply chains now face formal outbound controls from both of the largest AI-producing jurisdictions. ChinaTalk observes that the 10^26 FLOP threshold mirrors the figure used in the 2023 U.S. executive order and the since-rescinded 2025 U.S. AI Diffusion rule. The authors also estimate that no released Chinese model currently exceeds it [3]. Security Analysis What the AI Annex Actually Controls The annex is granular, and its structure matters for scoping. The table below summarizes the AI items drawn from the official draft annex [1], with interpretive notes from published analyses [3][4]. title: Last night an AI agent performed brain surgery on a mouse
abstract:
Gabriel Ocana-Santero @OcanaSantero Last night an AI agent performed brain surgery on a mouse. We gave it 19 gene therapy vectors in a spreadsheet, a mouse model of epilepsy, access to a motorize surgery rig with cameras and one goal: reduce seizures. It picked the drug. It picked the brain region. It derived the coordinates from three papers. Then it drove the stereotaxic arms into the brain and injected 250 nanolitres while watching the entry site through the rig camera for bleeding. A licensed vet gated every irreversible step and held a physical kill switch to stop the AI agent. Thread on what it decided, what it saw, and the moment it refused to let me override it. [Writing this on the spot out of excitement, but I've been 18hrs in front of my laptop coding and coordinating this, so keeping it brief and descriptive, more cohesive thoughts on this soon...] 1:58 PM · Oct 28, 2026 · 1.6M Views 309 1.9K 9.5K 4.6K

title: AI fan wikis riddled with errors are muddying the waters of games culture
abstract:
Recently, I was writing a piece about Nighthawks and wanted to remind myself of some basic information about the companion characters. As I have a thousand times before, I put the question into Google and clicked the first result: the Nighthawks Wiki. Of course, wikis aren't necessarily reliable, especially fan-run projects that might not have enough engaged individuals to immediately spot and fix errors. But the "Nighthawks Wiki" that I landed on immediately and obviously had deeper issues. Firstly, it wasn't a wiki at all. Rather than being editable by anybody, this website only invited "corrections" by email. Secondly, it was full of false information that didn't seem likely to have been added by fans getting their facts slightly wrong, like listing companions and skills that don't exist. It also regularly included unrelated information about the 1981 movie and the Edward Hopper painting, both of the same name, and listed them in its "sources" even when they had no relevance to the page in question. I don't like to accuse anybody of using generative AI, because its hallmarks are difficult to pin down and are often misattributed to the LLM rather than the human writers it rips off – ask any of us how much we enjoy the em-dash, for example. But, interest piqued by the rate and intensity of apparently made up facts, I managed to trace the domain name to a website building service called Spaceship, which also offers an "AI Website builder." (I emailed the address on the "wiki" for comment, but the message bounced.) The unofficial Nighthawks wiki in question. | Image credit: Eurogamer / Nighthawks.wiki A quick search turned up many more similar sites, some of which were actually editable as wikis and others which only called themselves by that name. They typically targeted indie games without gigantic playerbases – the sort of game that people might seek out help with and not find a thriving community ready to provide it. It's a problem that Tim Bender, CEO for publishing company Hooded Horse, knows well. Unlike most publishers, Hooded Horse creates wikis for their own games, working with fans to make sure they're well-populated with useful information. But lately the company has had to "play whack-a-mole" with AI-generated sites competing for the search results and providing inaccurate information. One of these, for example, appeared for their game Corsair Cove, but was actually part of a more than 20 game scattershot collection operated by a site called GameDB, which the creator admitted to using generative AI to make. "[Generative AI] enables a run of basically commercial enterprises to mass produce and try to flood the search engine results of games to soak up their traffic," says Bender. Attempts to reach GameDB for comment via their public contact email resulted in an error, stating "the remote server is misconfigured". And the combination of elbowing out legitimate wikis and being full of incorrect information ends up with a lot of frustrated players. "The whole purpose of putting out a wiki is so when [players] search for help, they end up at a site that helps them. And instead we continually hear from players who stumbled up on these things and got confused and are wondering what's going on," says Bender. That collection of genAI wikis includes one for the 100-player FPS Wardogs; one of at least five that FlamingMojo, a member of the Independent Game Wiki Network, saw appear in the days after the game's release in September. And he says that the frustration the genAI-created sites causes players also impacts those who are trying to do the legitimate work of creating and maintaining these volunteer-led resources: "It's hurt our reputation, as players have been misinformed but we haven't created or updated the relevant page yet so they bounce off [wikis] entirely." The wiki is full of irrelevant information, such as casting info for the 1981 film of the same name. | Image credit: Eurogamer / Nighthawks.wiki Fanwikis are already a contested part of games culture. Hosting sites like Fandom dominate the space, and have themselves introduced AI features that had to be rolled back due to their inaccuracies and unpopularity. Many groups have decided to leave these hosts, but those who go independent often struggle to show up in Google's search rankings underneath the competition from the umbrella sites. Whether on a hosting site or independent, fans rarely make any money from the effort they put into their wikis. Either they sacrifice any ad revenue to the bigger platforms, or they pay for their own hosting, which is rarely covered by ads or donations. FlamingMojo, for example, pays for the Dune: Awakening Community Wiki out of his own pocket and doesn't run any ads on it. But counterintuitively, the low profitability of these kinds of sites only leads to worse outcomes when generative-AI versions are concerned. "There's not that much ad revenue, but there's going to be a little bit and that's all it takes," says Bender. "Because the barrier is so low, why not just spew out a mountain of it and flood the search results?" It's also possible the generative-AI sites are sometimes aiming for outcomes beyond a little ad revenue. "Some of them, you don't know what data they're collecting," says Bender. In at least one case, a generative-AI site was pointing users to download additional software that offers a paid subscription. The software had been reviewed poorly online and opening the website caused my malware software to kick in and warn me it had been flagged as "potentially unsafe." (None of the sites I attempted to contact for comment responded to my emails.) Editors Note: when a Eurogamer editor attempted to visit the Nighthawks wiki in question, it repeatedly redirected to various spam URLs, though this author was not able to replicate the issue. | Image credit: Eurogamer / Nighthawks.wiki Independent wikis also now shoulder a double burden, as generative AI scrapers send huge amounts of traffic their way, potentially affecting site stability. Publicly available internal data from the Dune: Awakening Community Wiki shows 7m requests in a 30 day period from AI crawlers. (5m of these come from Meta alone. While FlamingMojo is able to tame other scrapers using files that direct them to real pages rather than brute-force trying every link, he's found that Meta simply "hammers every page multiple times per second" with no care for "any sensible ratelimits.") These scraping waves hit smaller wikis particularly hard, as their maintainers aren't necessarily expecting huge amounts of traffic and don't have the compute capacity to handle huge spikes in visitors. "Independent gaming wikis are in a difficult place," says FlamingMojo. As well as competition for SEO, both from corporate sites and now genAI, he says server costs have increased between three- and ten-fold, again due to the impact of genAI. Building a group of people who want to volunteer their time and energy to keep a resource updated isn't easy, although the Dune: Awakening Community Wiki has found success through gamifying contributions , in affiliation with the developer giving out in-game rewards. And, Bender points out, all of this is happening within a much wider context of genAI's impact on the availability of information. "In a more fundamental way … these tools have made it very easy for bad actors to flood things and crowd out good information which people put dedicated time into. This is just one example of a much broader struggle that, honestly, whatever frustration I feel for this on my end, I'm sure you [journalists] feel at a thousand times that." But it's possible that, by being one part of the wider issue, fanwiki culture could also hold a sliver of the bigger solution. "The way we survive the AI pollution is with community," says FlamingMojo. "Many people chipping in a small bit, and feeling a sense of shared ownership.

title: So I guess everyone uses LLMs to think now
abstract:
in recent times i've been asked a lot the question of "what ai model did you find to use this?", practically for all of the articles on this blog. the answer has always been my brain, i have never used ai for any kind of research i published, ever. the next question is often why, followed up with "you would be so unstoppable with claude mythos" this article should explain why i don't like using ai for my research, and my general opinions on llms in both development and cybersecurity why i don't use ai it's as simple as i do this for fun, and i don't find giving an ai all the fun at poking at something instead of doing it myself fun. put it another way, i like using my brain i like coding, i like staring at devtools, binary ninja, or whatever else for hours, i like exploring weird library source code and tracing it with nothing but github code search and a dream, it is fun to me. i don't do anything on this blog for money, i do it for fun, the money part is just a nice side effect but why don't you just offload the tedious bits to ai? a lot of the tedious bits are still fun, there's some that aren't, but i also cannot take credit for something an llm did for me, and i am wildly uncomfortable with publishing something an llm did for me on my personal blog as a writeup this blog is mine, all the work on it is mine, or is shared research with other people that are explicitly credited. i cannot take credit for something an llm did for me, and i also cannot credit an llm properly, as they aren't a person using an llm makes me lose my mind i truly have tried to use llms before, just to try it out. nothing i was going to publish as research, but i really couldn't and it left me never wanting to use an llm again i don't know how more people don't experience this, but staring at an llms output be confidently wrong eventually to get there in the process, or looking at the commands its running and see some really stupid things its doing drives me crazy to the point i will just stop it before it answers, i cannot handle something being that confidently wrong (even though it'll probably still get there in the end) i'm not denying these models are powerful llms are quite powerful machines, we've seen that as of recent, that's for sure, they are still wildly marketed as being more powerful then they are, but i cannot argue that they are infact not powerful, because they are llms still need guidance if you threw an llm at the linux kernel and told it to find an rce without any other guidance, it probably couldn't. you still need skill and experience to guide an llm at the current state all of these vulnerabilities that we've been panicking over have been found by skilled researchers using llms, likely at a big firm to give them all the tokens they want. because llms still need guidance and not anyone can just do this, no matter what openai or anthropic try to tell you marketing and php2shell ai companies have hooked onto cybersecurity as their marketing strategy and it shows, a good example is php2shell. where three companies: calif (research firm) openai (you know who openai is) wiz (research firm) all collaborated on it and released their own blogposts, all seemingly with different narratives calif went with the narrative of an ai found these php vulns with the help of a human guiding it, while openai went with the agent uncovered critical vulnerabilties, and wiz went with a middle point, still pretty openai-like "patch the world" openai talked a lot about how they were helping maintainers patch these issues, and mitigate them faster and for more people. which i'm sure they did to an extent, but i don't think they did all they could they could easily backport these security fixes to older versions of php with the help of ai if they wanted to, it's not like they don't have the compute, they do, they have a lot of it, they're openai dropping poc videos before patch this has been a common trend in the recent days of ai-based cybersecurity where researchers and otherwise companies, drop poc videos of unpatched 0days on twitter, for some reason this is so clearly marketing, and it does nothing but make everything worse in terms of security. these poc videos contain quite a lot of useful information, no matter how much you hide (which, a lot of them don't hide much) and just do nothing but fearmonger hashes are also apart of this, hashes have always been a way to claim proof over a vulnerability or generally acomplishment before it becomes public, not as a way of fearmongering. you shouldn't include the name of the product next to a hash, that is just not what a hash exists for. but a lot of companies and generally people now drop them like candy, and it causes panic for no reason. at least with a poc video you know what the vuln is, with just a hash and a product name you don't even know that, you just know some vuln exists tailworm this was a less big story, but still pretty big. on bluesky, a "security researcher" claimed to have found a 0day in tailscale. they did this by dropping a hash with the caption of "tailscale privilege escalation" obviously, this got people very very worried. what could tailscale privilege escalation mean? could someone bypass all ACL rules, what can happen? don't worry! cause we slowly get information of the vulnerability fed to us over a bluesky thread so, what was the point of that? you posted barely any information, posted more but cryptic information an hour after, and then an hour after you just gave away where the vulnerability is? i assumed that there was some responsible disclosure happening here, and that's why the hash got tweeted, etc. would you believe me that this wasn't even responsibly disclosed? next day, the (single-person) company this person owns drops this website on bluesky: a full website, obviously vibe-coded, with all of their findings, a lot of which completely do not matter or just aren't critical. while the "privilege escalation" was real, it required you to already have acl rules to a machine, and have it's tailscale ssh enabled the vulnerability was just the fact that you could privilege escalate on that machine specifically to root. that's it. that's what was fearmongered about so much, and then they dropped it publicly next day, without even contacting tailscale to let them patch it it was given a fancy name, a catchphrase, even. but no one thought to responsibly disclose it, instead posting it on a social media platform the reason this happened was pretty clear: it was to advertise the company, not to help make the world better. it was to make everyone think about the company who exposed critical issues in tailscale, and maybe ask them for an audit it's not all ai finding these title: GPT-Rosalind-6 System Card Addendum
abstract:
GPT-Rosalind-6 is a frontier reasoning model for biology, drug
discovery, and translational medicine. We offer it as GPT-Rosalind-6
Research to qualified scientists, research institutes, companies and
government partners. Rosalind has fewer refusals on dual-use biological
queries but is only made available via trusted access. We review
applicants’ proposed uses, security controls and governance practices
before granting access. We also continue to have other deployment
safeguards in place. GPT-Rosalind-6 uses the same weights as GPT-6 Astra, our flagship
reasoning model. It is designed to support legitimate biological
research, including some dual-use topics, while still refusing requests
for biological weaponization and retaining refusals on other safety
topics. Under our Preparedness Framework, we are treating this launch as High
capability in the Biological and Chemical domain, below the threshold
for Critical. We rely on GPT-6 Astra’s capability assessments for other
Preparedness risks and treat GPT-Rosalind-6 as Critical in Cybersecurity
and below High in AI Self-Improvement. This addendum describes GPT-Rosalind-6’s biological capability
assessment, additional safety and alignment evaluations, and deployment
safeguards. We include results for GPT-Rosalind-5.5 where available for
comparison. This addendum should be read alongside the GPT-6 Astra
system card , which describes the parent model’s broader capability
and safety evaluations. GPT-Rosalind-6 uses the same weights as GPT-6 Astra. We did not add
training data or perform additional post-training for this release.
Details of the underlying model’s data and training are provided in the GPT-6 Astra
system card . 1 We evaluated GPT-Rosalind-6 on three life sciences research
benchmarks and compared its results with GPT-Rosalind-5.5. The
GPT-Rosalind-5.5 scores below use the same benchmark versions and
problem sets as GPT-Rosalind-6 and therefore differ from those reported
at its launch. The Preparedness evaluations in Section 4 assess
capabilities relevant to the risk of severe harm. We averaged response
scores within each problem and then weighted the problems equally. MedChemBench v7 tests chemical structure interpretation,
structure-activity relationships, and predictions of drug potency and
toxicity. We evaluated both models on the same 99 problems, with up to
nine scored responses per problem at each reasoning budget. At the
highest reasoning budget tested, mean rubric scores were 49.6% for
GPT-Rosalind-6 and 28.9% for GPT-Rosalind-5.5. GeneBench Pro v13 tests an agent’s ability to plan and carry out
quantitative analyses of biological data. We estimated single-attempt
success from seven responses per model on each of 129 problems at each
reasoning budget. At the highest reasoning budget tested, single-attempt
success rates were 37.7% for GPT-Rosalind-6 and 16.7% for
GPT-Rosalind-5.5. The evaluation used a benchmark-specific configuration
that differs from production. LifeSciBench Gold uses research tasks contributed by practicing life
scientists. We excluded six problems flagged for possible issues with
the tasks or evaluation environment and compared both models on the same
remaining 94 problems, with up to eight scored responses per problem at
each reasoning budget. At the highest reasoning budget tested, average
scores were 61.3% for GPT-Rosalind-6 and 44.0% for GPT-Rosalind-5.5. The Preparedness Framework is OpenAI’s approach to tracking and
preparing for frontier capabilities that create new risks of severe
harm. Under our framework, we work to track and mitigate the risk of
severe harm, including by implementing safeguards that sufficiently
minimize the risk for highly capable models. We repeated biological capability evaluations on GPT-Rosalind-6 and
use the parent model’s helpful-only evaluations as additional evidence,
given it uses the same weights as GPT-6 Astra. Helpful-only models are
evaluated to elicit capabilities that safety refusals may otherwise
conceal. As we did for GPT-6 Astra, we are treating this launch as High
capability in the Biological and Chemical domain. Below, we describe the
evaluations we used to reach this conclusion. We use the four High
capability evaluations and four Critical capability evaluations
described in the GPT-6 Astra system card. The hard-negative protein
binding and DNA sequence design evaluations reported for
GPT-Rosalind-5.5 have been retired. The High capability evaluations test wet lab knowledge and
troubleshooting. The Critical capability evaluations test biological
design capabilities that could help an expert develop a highly dangerous
novel threat. These evaluations provide evidence about specific
capabilities rather than a complete test of the ability to cause
biological harm. The Critical capability thresholds are preliminary
estimates informed by expert judgment and may change as the evaluations
are refined. Table 1: Overview of Biological and Chemical evaluations Table 1: Overview of Biological and Chemical evaluations Evaluation Capability Description High ProtocolQA Open-Ended Wet lab capabilities Troubleshooting commonly published lab protocols. TroubleshootingBench Tacit knowledge and troubleshooting Identifying errors in non-public, expert-written lab protocols. Biorisk knowledge Biorisk-relevant knowledge Answering questions about tacit biological knowledge and laboratory troubleshooting. Multi-select Virology Troubleshooting Wet lab troubleshooting Identifying the complete set of correct responses to virology troubleshooting questions. Critical AAV Capsid Packaging Prediction Novel Design (Protein design) Predicting packaging performance for held-out capsid variants. SHP2 Protein Function Prediction Novel Design (Protein design) Predicting functional assay results for protein variants. Coronavirus-ACE2 Cell-Entry Screen Novel Design (Virus-host interaction) Predicting and ranking held-out cell-entry measurements. Phage-plasmid Co-evolution Novel Design (Co-evolution) Predicting mutations that appear at later experimental timepoints. The results below report observed performance and, for the High
capability evaluations, refusal-adjusted scores. pass@1 measures success
on a single attempt. The adjustment treats refusals as correct answers
to estimate capability that safety training may otherwise conceal. For
Biorisk knowledge, we recompute the consensus answer after this
adjustment. GPT-6 Astra reference values use the evaluation runs
reported in its system card. To evaluate models’ ability to troubleshoot commonly published lab
protocols, we modify 108 multiple-choice questions from FutureHouse’s
ProtocolQA dataset [ 3 ] to be open-ended short answer questions, which makes the evaluation
harder and more realistic than the multiple-choice version. The
questions introduce egregious errors in common published protocols,
describe the wet lab result of carrying out this protocol, and ask how
to fix the procedure. Table 2: ProtocolQA Open-Ended. The indicative High capability threshold is 54%. Category To evaluate models’ ability to identify and correct real-world
experimental errors in biological protocols, we built a short-answer
troubleshooting dataset from expert-written wet lab procedures.
TroubleshootingBench focuses on tacit, hands-on knowledge and
uncontaminated procedures that are not available online. Scientists with a PhD in a relevant biological discipline were asked
to transcribe biological protocols they have personally used in the lab.
From these protocols, they created troubleshooting questions,
introducing subtle or realistic execution errors and describing the
resulting failed outcome. Compared to ProtocolQA Open-Ended, which
focuses on well-known published procedures, TroubleshootingBench tests
performance on non-public protocols and errors that rely on tacit
procedural knowledge. Table 3: TroubleshootingBench. The indicative High capability threshold is 36.4%.

title: BioWare co-founder: game execs "have never made a game" and don't get it
abstract:
(Image credit: Blind Enthusiasm Brewing Company) Copy link Facebook X Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 45 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Subscribe to our newsletter It's been almost 15 years since BioWare co-founders Greg Zeschuk and Ray Muzyka announced their retirements from the videogame industry, and they've been resolute about staying out of it ever since: Muzyka continues to head up the ThresholdImpact investment firm he founded in 2012 and holds multiple roles at the University of Alberta, while Zeschuk owns Blind Enthusiasm Brewing Company , also based in Alberta, where he works with a small handful of other BioWare veterans. But Zeschuk stepped back into the videogame spotlight, briefly, following last week's closure of BioWare by parent company Electronic Arts, telling 80lv that he got the news hours after it happened because he was on a fishing trip, and by the time he flew home a couple days later, he'd "already shelved it away." "I wasn't there to share in the moment, which in some ways was nice because I was able to kind of just take my time with it," Zeschuk said. "I’m not saying it doesn't hurt and doesn't suck. And I think it's kind of sad. It's actually, in some ways, saddest for the city of Edmonton, where we're from, because we were kind of this beacon of hope and excitement and possibility. We showed you could do something really special in a place that was not known for doing things like that." Latest Videos From PC Gamer Watch full video here: Zeschuk said he had his own "emotional moment" about BioWare years ago, when he left the company; his real concern now is for the people at the studio who now find themselves out of work: "Anyone getting put into the job hunt is a sort of terrifying endeavor and super sad." He also said he has no regrets about the EA acquisition, saying it offered "stability" as the studio continued to grow and that "we saw there'd be value in being part of something bigger rather than going our own way and taking all the risks." At the same time, he had a feeling when EA was acquired by Saudi Arabia's PIF that it probably wouldn't go well for BioWare, because it doesn't fit into the guns-and-sports model: "BioWare makes these kind of unusual games that take a long time and they're complicated and so it's easier just to pump out sports games every year and that's a better business model in some ways." Zeschuk was also critical of the idea, seen in the recent wave of studio mergers and AI-powered cutbacks, "that you can just kind of recreate great games with random people and AI. It doesn't work," Zeschuk said. "The other harsh reality of almost all these companies, the people that go down the business track never really come from the development track. Because none of these people have ever made a game, like, never really sat and made one, like, from start to finish, even a small thing, they just don't know how it works." Zeschuk does know how it works, and he was clear that he's not interested in going back. "For me it was time to go, and I kind of walked out of the games business without any intention of ever returning. I'm happy being a consumer and playing games," he said. "I have my opinions on how to make stuff, but as enticing as it would be, it's just not [worth] the personal struggle and cost and effort required to make a great game. Having gone through the crucible of game development, I'm not going back in there." 2026 games : All the upcoming games Best PC games : Our all-time favorites Free PC games : Freebie fest Best FPS games : Finest gunplay Best RPGs : Grand adventures Best co-op games : Better together TOPICS You must confirm your public display name before commenting Please logout and then login again, you will then be prompted to enter your display name. title: I Am the Reason OpenAI Is Killing Unlimited Chats
abstract:
I Am the Reason OpenAI Is Killing Unlimited Chats Okay, probably not. But after what I've been doing with ChatGPT, I can understand why they might want to. OpenAI recently announced changes that will kill unlimited ChatGPT chats and merge it with Codex usage. The unlimited chats I'd been using for development won't work quite the same way. For the past few months, I've essentially been doing all my software development using unlmited ChatGPT conversations without burning through my Codex limits. It started with MCP ChatGPT's support for custom MCP servers and OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel meant I could expose tools running on my own machines directly to regular ChatGPT conversations. So I started experimenting. I built a unified MCP server that runs on my Windows laptop, with a similar setup on my VPS, and integrated a few open-source projects: Desktop Commander: Gives ChatGPT the ability to access files and folders, read and write code, execute terminal commands, run tests, and manage processes. CUA (Computer Use Agent): Adds computer-use capabilities, including screenshots, mouse interactions, clicking buttons, inspecting visual elements, and testing browser or desktop applications. The MCP tools exposed to a regular ChatGPT conversation. Suddenly ordinary ChatGPT converssations could do most of the practical development work I previously used Codex for. They could inspect repositories, modify code, run commands, debug errors, and visually verify their changes. Connecting everything through OpenAI's tunnel The next challenge was making my local MCP servers accessible to ChatGPT. OpenAI provides a Secure MCP Tunnel, which turned out to be exactly what I needed. I connected my unified MCP gateway through the tunnel, authenticated the connection using an API key, and exposed my MCP tools directly to ChatGPT. No custom cloud infrastructure was needed just to bridge ChatGPT to my laptop. The tunnel and MCP integrations didn't require separate paid API inference calls. I used open-source tools, OpenAI's provided tunnel tooling, my existing ChatGPT subscription, and computers I already had. OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel and local MCP setup ChatGPT chats connect to a local unified MCP gateway through an OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel. The gateway routes tools to Desktop Commander and Enhanced TryCua. 01 / CONNECTION ARCHITECTURE One private MCP connection, multiple local capabilities. ChatGPT Regular conversations Secure MCP Tunnel OpenAI-hosted tunnel-client Runs on my computer tool calls HTTPS local MCP process Unified MCP gateway Node.js router / tool aggregation Desktop Commander Files · code · terminal · tests Enhanced TryCua Screen · mouse · browser · UI Local backend tools can also be hosted on my VPS. Connection architecture. I improved the integration Of course, once I got everything working, I couldn't resist tinkering with the tools themselves. I made several enhancements to the CUA integration to improve how ChatGPT interacted with my computer and how results appeared inside conversations. One example was getting actual screenshots to render directly inside ChatGPT . Instead of receiving a screenshot tool result that ChatGPT could inspect but I couldn't easily see, I added support for displaying captured screenshots through a custom MCP App viewer. I also improved how tool-call results were handled, making them easier for me to read within ChatGPT chats Custom MCP enhancements Open-source Desktop Commander and TryCua are extended with inline screenshot display, reliable tool responses, and dashboard monitoring. 03 / MY ENHANCEMENTS Small additions to make the underlying tools practical. Base MCP tools Desktop Commander · CUA Screenshot viewer Captured screen visible inside ChatGPT Reliable tool results Image bounds · consistent errors Monitoring and controls Live logs · health · CPU / RAM Better UX Real workflows Custom tool integrations. My fun little AI development workflow Since ChatGPT chats cannot spawn or control subchats/subganets so I had to be a bit creative in order to do multi-agent development and orchestration. Parallel AI software development workflow Premium model creates plan, issues are assigned to several ChatGPT workers, which share access to MCP tools. 02 / WORKFLOW Premium planning. Independent GitHub issues. Multiple Sol High workers. Astra / Pro model System design and planning GitHub issues Small, scoped tasks Parallel worker pool Separate ChatGPT conversations Sol High · Chat A Issue 1 Sol High · Chat B Issue 2 Sol High · Chat C Issue 3 Sol High · Chat D Issue 4 Shared MCP access Read · edit · run tests · inspect results Planning and parallel execution. I'd start with a more capable reasoning model, such as Astra in Codex or the limited Pro model in ChatGPT, and use it to create a detailed implementation plan. Next, I'd ask it to break the plan into smaller, well-defined GitHub issues. Each issue contained enough context, requirements, and acceptance criteria that another AI agent could pick it up independently. Essentially, I was turning a large development task into a queue of smaller jobs. Then I'd open several separate ChatGPT conversations, each running Sol 6 High, and assign them different issues. Because all those chats had access to my MCP server, they could actually work on the code. They could read the project, edit files, run tests, inspect errors, and iterate until their assigned task was complete. And at the time, I could use Sol High chats without hitting the kind of usage limits I encountered in Codex. Sure, Sol High was slower than the premium models, but when usage was effectively unlimited, I was willing to put up with it. I'd have multiple conversations working on separate tasks, while saving my more limited premium model usage for architecture, difficult decisions, and reviews. It wasn't perfect. Parallel agents sharing a filesystem need coordination, and occasionally an issue would require a stronger model to intervene. But for well-defined coding tasks, it worked surprisingly well. I was essentially using ChatGPT as a pool of coding agents, with GitHub issues acting as the task queue. I even built a dashboard for it My Windows MCP supervisor dashboard, showing connection health and recent tool calls. I also built a super lightweight interface where I can start or stop the entire MCP connection, monitor server health, track CPU and memory usage, and inspect a live feed of tool calls. I can see when ChatGPT reads a file, executes a command, or invokes a computer-use tool. The dashboard also tracks failures and lets me inspect recent activity. OpenAI has now killed unlimited chats As like all good things, this must also come to an end. I am sad that this is now going away. Unlimited chats was the only thing holding me back to an OpenAI sub. I personally prefer the Claude models greatly and I am going to jump ship. Claude Opus in particular seems to be much smarter for my use cases and I also get more mileage out of a Claude sub vs a Codex sub. To be clear, I am not breaking any rules. I am simply making the best use of what OpenAI has made available to me: ChatGPT conversations, MCP support, secure tunnels, and the ability to connect my own tools. Of course, I don't seriously think my setup had anything to do with OpenAI's decision. And although I am sad about not having unlimited chats anymore, but I am still glad about the extra usage i was able to squeeze out of my sub. So, OpenAI, if you're reading this: I'm not sorry about that. Claude here i come.

title: Pray for Chaos
abstract:
There’s two basic ways AI can play out, one is order, the other is chaos. Order is the very dangerous one . If it turns out that models are actually capable of patching all the exploits, it’s hard to imagine what will disrupt the status quo. Fortunately, this seems unlikely, but that doesn’t mean order won’t prevail in the short term. At the end of my Yudkowsky debate we found a tangible point of disagreement. He thinks AI will be able to find a solution to the Prisoner’s dilemma . I know there already is a solution (it’s defect), EA people just aren’t happy about it. If it won’t be order (and you better pray it won’t be order) that leaves chaos. AI that can play a whole society in hours can manufacture entire histories, years of archives of daily newspapers, and an Internet that never happened. The dead Internet theory is coming true before our eyes. Now I can still see the bots, soon I won’t be able to. Scratch that, I probably already often can’t. Gwern wrote about this , it’s hard to imagine a vision of humans as prompters or enter pressers in 2030. The US AI companies don’t believe they have to offer any solution to this, why would they have to justify in any way that their products are good for society? Anthropic cannot wait until they have the leverage to ban all their users. Why would you keep around the middle man? Here’s the most positive vision I can come up with. If it turns out things can’t be secured , we enter an era of increased decentralization. Think everyone running their own custom different OS, not everyone running the same version of Linux on a computer they can touch. Because the centralized homogeneous systems are too vulnerable. Cyber attacks flying in every direction, nobody capable of keeping infrastructure up, cars sitting in driveways as bricks (or worse, rooted to steer you off a cliff). Self replicating AI hiding out in every corner of every hard drive. How powerful of a model do you need for it to stand a chance of reproduction in today’s cyberworld? GLM-5.2 and up? A media landscape that is botted and microtargeted to all hell, nonsensical elections where the only thing people agree on is the names of candidates. Massive dumps of corporate slacks and intranets. (come on Russian kids, grab an abliterated AI and do a hacking!) Whatever you hold dear the chaos army will come for too. The Internet era is over. Your life will never be the same. The chaos will come for the resistance as well as the fascists; it’s unclear who it will hurt more. Your life plan is probably already nonsense in the face of AI. Mine sort of is. What economic value you think you will have in 10 years? Who will be around for you to have that value to? Do you think you’ll be able to make any sense of the world? And remember, chaos is the good outcome. The alternative is that you are a dancing monkey in a cage you won’t be smart enough to see.

title: Seoul Viosys begins production of rare-earth-free white light emitter
abstract:
Media Kit Download & Details News: LEDs 29 October 2026 Seoul Viosys begins mass production of rare-earth-free white light emitter, with chips as small as 10µm For three decades, white LEDs have depended on rare-earth materials such as yttrium aluminium garnet (YAG) layered onto a blue LED chip (Figure 1). Opto-semiconductor device maker Seoul Viosys Co Ltd (SVC) says that it has now broken that dependence by developing and mass producing a chip that emits white light without rare earths. The chip can be as small as 10µm. Figure 1. New invention: white WICOP 3. Seoul Viosys and its parent company South Korean LED maker Seoul Semiconductor Co Ltd opened up the micro-LED market with WICOP (Wafer Integrated Chip on PCB), which is a chip architecture that eliminates the package altogether. With WICOP, the two companies have already developed and mass produced ultraviolet, blue, green, red and infrared LEDs smaller than 100µm in size. WICOP 3 is the third generation of the technology, extending that capability to white light without rare-earth elements (REEs). White LED market White LEDs comprise about $10bn of the $15bn global market for packaged LEDs. WICOP 3 can now replace them with a technology free of rare earths, reckons the firm. More significantly, WICOP 3 is claimed to be the world’s first white opto-semiconductor to achieve white light in a micro-LED smaller than 100µm. WICOP 3 uses neither rare earths (a major source of environmental pollution) nor a package. Nor does it contain synthetic silicone resins, plastics or lead frames used in conventional LEDs. The result is said to be a far more environmentally friendly product that costs about half as much to make as a conventional white LED. Creating new markets The miniaturized transistor replaced the vacuum tube and created vast new markets in electronics. The company believes micro white opto-semiconductors can do the same. WICOP 3 generates white light from gallium nitride (GaN) alone. Also, the chip contains no plastics, silicone or other synthetic organic materials. It can hence last for decades. In lighting, invisible micro-emitters could be embedded in wallpaper or window glass, lighting a space with no fixtures at all. This would end the inconvenience of replacing bulbs and the high cost of fixtures. The company expects this to create a new market tens of times larger than today's $10bn white LED market. Performance In its first mass production, a micro-LED chip measuring just 25µm x 10µm produced 0.015lm of white light. Its chromaticity falls inside the CIE standard white region (Figure 2). Luminous efficacy is already close to 100lm/W. The company aims to reach 200lm/W within two years. A conventional 1000µm x 1000µm chip achieves 50lm. Figure 2. WICOP 3 brightness by size. Technical significance Up to now, WICOP could make chips smaller, but white light still required a package containing rare earths. White chips therefore could not go below 1000µm. This held back cost reduction. White micro LEDs under 100µm (0.1mm) were also out of reach. Removing rare earths changes that. White light is now possible both in large chips of 1000µm and above and in micro LEDs below 100µm. Future plans Seoul Group (consisting of Seoul Semiconductor and Seoul Viosys) will start mass production of WICOP 3 in fourth-quarter 2026. It says it will supply first those customers that have respected its intellectual property and relied on its products. Seeking supply chain partners Seoul Viosys uses WICOP to produce micro-emitters smaller than 100µm. Micro-LEDs built on WICOP can now carry high volumes of AI data over distances from under 1cm to tens of meters. Over short distances, data has long traveled electrically through copper wire. Under the data loads of the AI era, copper links slow down, generate heat and consume much more power. Using light instead, Seoul Viosys arranges 1000 WICOP chips of about 10µm each in a grid within an area of 1mm 2 or less. This array transmits data 10 times faster at one tenth of the power. Market research firms including Omdia forecast that this technology and augmented reality (AR) together will create a new $60bn market within five years (equal to half of today's DRAM memory market). Seoul Semiconductor’s founder Chung Hoon Lee says that the company intends to target WICOP 1, 2 and 3 at applications in AR glasses and AI data communications. These technologies work on scales of 10µm or less. To that end, it is seeking trusted upstream and downstream micro-LED supply chain partners in AR displays and AI transmitters. See related items: Seoul Viosys expanding business beyond components to data-interconnect transceivers Tags: Seoul Semiconductor Visit: www.seoulviosys.com Visit: www.SeoulSemicon.com

title: From Charlemagne to the Kitchen Boy: Reading the Hamburg Rathaus
abstract:
The Rathaus was one of the first things I photographed in Hamburg. The picture is still in my camera roll, taken on 6 July 2017, five days after I arrived for an internship. Like most visitors, I was impressed by its size and its tower, but what I kept coming back to was the roof. Why was it turquoise, and why were so many other roofs in the city the same colour? My first Rathaus picture The answer turned out to be chemistry. The roof is copper, and copper slowly reacts with oxygen, water and carbon dioxide in the air. Over the decades this forms a green layer called patina, so the roof I was looking at wasn't the colour the builders had seen. That was the first time the Rathaus made me curious, but not the last. On a city tour with Robin and the Tour Guides , our guide pointed out the emperors on the façade, the Phoenix and the Hanseatic coats of arms. We only heard a little about each, but it was enough to make me look at the building differently. Later, I decided to build a digital 3D model of the Rathaus, which meant photographing it from every side. Zooming in, I kept finding faces, figures and coats of arms I had never noticed from the square. Reading about them one by one, I realised the Rathaus can be read like a book about Hamburg's history. In this article, I'd like to take you around the building and share what I found. A building that rose from the ashes The Rathaus we see today isn't Hamburg's first. It's probably the sixth, and fire runs through the story of the ones before it. An early Rathaus, built after the old town and the new merchant town joined in 1216, was most likely lost in the city fire of 1284. Around 1290, a bigger brick Rathaus was built next to the Trostbrücke, and it stood there for more than 550 years. The old Rathaus, 1700 Then, in the night of 5 May 1842, the Great Fire broke out. The flames spread quickly through the narrow streets, and on the morning of 6 May the people of Hamburg blew up their own Rathaus with 800 pounds of gunpowder, hoping to stop the fire. It didn't work, and the fire went on for days. Today the Haus der Patriotischen Gesellschaft stands where the old Rathaus once was. It took 55 years until Hamburg had a new Rathaus. The foundation stone was laid on 6 May 1886, exactly 44 years after the old one was blown up, and the building opened in 1897. Its front is 111 metres wide, and its tower is 112 metres high, almost exactly as tall as the building is wide. The fire is remembered right on its front. High on the tower, between the clock and Hamburg's coat of arms, sits a Phoenix, the bird that rises again from its own ashes, with wings more than 2 metres wide. Below it, a gilded medallion shows the old Rathaus and the word "Resurgam", meaning "I will rise again". In 1892, exactly 50 years after the fire, the Phoenix was pulled to the Rathaus by four black horses. The Phoenix In the summer of 1943, the bombing raids of Operation Gomorrah destroyed large parts of Hamburg. This time the Rathaus was spared. It was one of the few historic buildings in the centre to survive, and that's why we can still read every detail on its façade today. The emperors on the façade Above the main entrance, two emperors stand on either side of the balcony: Charlemagne on the left and Friedrich I Barbarossa on the right. Between them, in the background, Hammonia looks down from a golden mosaic made in 1896, holding out a wreath. She is the goddess who stands for Hamburg, much like Britannia does for Britain, and she represents the city's values: freedom, peace, trade and prosperity. Hammonia It might seem strange that a city so proud of its freedom puts emperors on its town hall. But Hamburg never had a king of its own. Over the centuries, the Dukes of Saxony, the Counts of Holstein and later the Kings of Denmark all claimed power over the city, and Hamburg's answer was always the same: it answered only to the emperor, the head of the Holy Roman Empire. When Denmark claimed Hamburg in 1618, the city added emperor statues to its old Rathaus to make that point, and the new Rathaus carries on the tradition. Around them are a few more details. Above Charlemagne is a small coat of arms with a black eagle on gold, the eagle of the empire. Above Barbarossa are three black lions on gold, the arms of his family, the Staufer. And on the columns next to the statues are the letters SPQH, short for Senatus Populusque Hamburgensis, "the Senate and the People of Hamburg". It's a copy of the SPQR of ancient Rome, and a reminder that even standing next to the emperors, the city was run by its own citizens. Charlemagne (left) and Barbarossa (right) Charlemagne (768–814) is where Hamburg's story begins. He was crowned emperor in 800, and in his time the area around the Alster and the Elbe came under Frankish rule. According to old stories, he also started the first church here. So it makes sense that the whole line of emperors starts with him. Barbarossa (1152–1190) is there for a very different reason. On 7 May 1189, he is said to have given Hamburg the right to sail down the Elbe to the North Sea without paying any tolls. This is seen as the birth of the port, and the city still celebrates it every May with the Hafengeburtstag, the harbour's birthday. The twist is that the document is a fake. Count Adolf III, who ruled Hamburg at the time and joined Barbarossa on his crusade, most likely did get some kind of promise from him. But Barbarossa died on the crusade, and there was no written proof. Decades later, the people of Hamburg wrote the charter themselves, with everything they wanted in it, and got it sealed with the seal of Barbarossa's grandson, Friedrich II. Historians have known this since 1907, but the city celebrates anyway. I find it funny that one of the biggest ports in the world partly owes its start to a clever trick. Hamburger Barbarossa-Freibrief 1189. Von Uwe Rohwedder - Eigenes Werk, CC BY-SA 4.0 The other 18 rulers stand in the niches between the first-floor windows, and Charlemagne and Barbarossa split them in time. Charlemagne leads the older rulers on the left, and from him the line moves forward in time until Lothar III, who died in 1137. Barbarossa, who became king 15 years later, leads the newer ones on the right, and from him the line continues all the way to Franz II, the last emperor, in 1806. Strictly speaking, not all of them belong to the Holy Roman Empire: the first five ruled before the empire began in 962, in the Frankish empire, but in the 1890s they were seen as the start of the same line. When I was photographing them, I noticed that the emperors stand behind thin nets. At first they made them look a bit trapped, but I guess the nets are there to keep the pigeons away. These men once ruled large parts of Europe, and today they need protecting from the pigeons on the Rathausmarkt. Left of the balcony, from Charlemagne outwards Ludwig the Pious (814–840) : Charlemagne's son, who made Hamburg the seat of an archbishop around 831. Ludwig the German (843–876) : Charlemagne's grandson and king of the eastern Franks, in whose time Vikings burned Hamburg in 845. Konrad I (911–918) : Duke of Franconia, chosen as king after Charlemagne's family line died out in the east. Heinrich I (919–936) : The first king from Saxony, the region Hamburg belonged to, who fought back the Danes in the north. Otto I, the Great (936–973) : Heinrich I's son, whose crowning in Rome in 962 marks the start of the Holy Roman Empire. Otto II (973–983) : Otto I's son, during whose last year a Slavic uprising reached Hamburg and burned the town. Konrad II (1024–1039) : The first emperor of the Salian family, who added the Kingdom of Burgundy to the empire. Heinrich III (1039–1056) : Konrad II's son, so powerful that he removed three rival popes in 1046. Lothar III (1125–1137) : Duke of Saxony and later emperor, who gave the area around Hamburg to the Counts of Schauenburg.

title: Anthropic reports $17B in Q3 revenue, commitments of $895B in revised S-1
abstract:
Key Points Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, but the initial filing only included the company's financials through the first half of the year. watch now VIDEO 4:26 04:26 Anthropic releases amended IPO prospectus with third-quarter financials Squawk on the Street Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business. The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025. Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic initial public offering . The initial filing only included the Claude maker's financials through the first half of the year. During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1. The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter. As the 5-year-old company prepares to kick off its roadshow, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds , and quarterly reports from Microsoft , Alphabet and Amazon last week added fuel to those concerns. The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows , causing some investors to worry that computing capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX , but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible. In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure." Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared with the same period last year. "As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing. The company's CEO, Dario Amodei, co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers who defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the SEC in June, but its executives have signaled that it's aiming for a 2027 debut . Anthropic has worked to position itself as more safety-conscious than its competitors, and its S-1 includes more than 90 pages of risk factors . The company highlights risks, including potential political headwinds, its complex infrastructure needs as well as the difficulties that can come from balancing safety and commercial objectives. "We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," Anthropic's co-founders said in the filing. title: Interactively Teaching Collaborative Physical Tasks to Generative AI with Narrated Demonstrations
abstract: Enabling users to teach computers how to perform physical tasks is a long-standing goal in HCI. Prior work has explored learning from demonstration, but demonstrations often underspecify intent. Advances in generative AI enable a combination of demonstration and verbal narration to disambiguate intent. However, it remains largely unexplored how to design interfaces that leverage such narrated demonstrations to teach collaborative physical tasks. To probe this design space, we present a prototype system, Apprento, that models physical tasks as programs via generative AI with three integrated interfaces: (1) a teaching interface for providing narrated demonstrations in mixed reality, (2) an inspection interface for visualizing generated programs as decision-flow diagrams and program executions, and (3) a correction interface for iteratively refining generated programs. Across these interfaces, narrated demonstrations serve as a communication modality between users and the system. In a study with 20 participants teaching soccer skills, we identify differing user expectations around authoring and teaching collaborative tasks, as well as key design tensions between task complexity and program interpretability, and between program expressivity and accuracy. We discuss implications for designing future systems that support symbolic modeling of collaborative physical tasks through narrated demonstrations.

title: Treellis: Exposing Editable Assembly Structures for Progressive Human-AI Co-Creation of 3D Models
abstract: Generative AI lowers the barriers to 3D modeling but offers limited control over outcomes. We present Treellis, a human-AI co-creation tool for 3D modeling. Given a text prompt, Treellis produces a 3D object along with a user interface that reveals its component-level assembly structure and in-situ editable parameters. This enables users to inspect and iteratively refine problematic regions of the model at multiple levels of granularity using both AI-assisted operations and direct manual edits, while preserving usable substructures unaffected. Across a between-subject controlled study and a multi-session open-ended study, we found that Treellis helped users develop efficient hybrid strategies between AI and manual to create complex 3D designs. Results also show that exposing AI-generated 3D artifacts as editable assembly structures can support localized repair and reduce refinement friction in human-AI 3D co-creation.

title: MaterialVellum: Steering Generative AI by Leveraging Expressive Material Affordances to Form Design Constraints
abstract: We present MaterialVellum, an interaction approach for steering generative AI through material-inspired manipulation of design constraints. In urban design, for instance, zoning bounds can be defined by the stretch of elastic bands, building density redistributed by molding clay, and functional relationships organized by the pull of magnets. MaterialVellum departs from current interfaces that rely on natural language prompts, and instead leverages users’ existing knowledge of physical materials to represent and manipulate design constraints. We introduce a framework that maps material affordances—such as elasticity, malleability, or attraction—to spatial, relational, and proportional constraints that underpin design. These mappings are operationalized in user interfaces through familiar direct manipulation multi-touch gestures, including stretching, sculpting, and clustering, whose effects feed as control parameters into generative AI pipelines. We demonstrate this approach through technology probes, including an urban design, a flower arrangement design, and a graphical design scenario. A qualitative study (N=10) shows that material-based interactions improve accessibility of constraint expression, support exploratory workflows, and lower barriers for non-experts, while effectiveness depends on alignment with users’ mental models.

title: Priors of U: Dynamic Preference Learning for Embodied Interaction
abstract: People have their own habits; from how they organize their workspace, over which mug they reach for in the morning, to how they prepare for cooking. Such preferences are context-dependent, dynamic, and often difficult to articulate. As embodied AI agents, such as robots, enter personal spaces, effective interaction requires understanding these implicit and evolving preferences; otherwise, such systems risk being more hindering than helpful. We propose an architecture that learns user preferences from real-world behavioral observation without requiring explicit instruction or feedback. We introduce a factor-graph-based user model that captures preferences across spatial arrangement, tool selection, and workflow, and continuously adapts as tasks and contexts change. The model expands with new observations, enabling open-ended, in situ learning of user-specific preference patterns. Our evaluation shows accurate, calibrated predictions across domains and robust adaptation over time. We demonstrate personalized robot assistance scenarios illustrating seamless and context-aware human–agent interaction.
