title: Veriscope: Provenance-Aware Verification of LLM Reasoning Artifacts in Conversational Data Analysis
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adopted by data analysts to perform various analytical tasks within conversational interfaces, owing to their capabilities in code generation and analytical reasoning. Conversational LLMs generate diverse artifacts through multiple reasoning steps and summarize analytical results into insights. Verifying such analysis remains essential yet challenging, as it requires examining both diverse artifacts and the underlying complex reasoning logic, which is not fully addressed by previous work. To facilitate validating LLM-generated results, we present a claim-centered view of analytic provenance and introduce Veriscope, an interactive system that supports fine-grained verification across interconnected artifacts, on-demand tracing of analytic provenance, and modification of analytical results. We formulated our design considerations based on findings derived from a formative study conducted with data analysts (N=6) who have prior experience in verification. We evaluated the effectiveness and usability of our method through a user study (N=18), which demonstrated that Veriscope substantially improves the efficiency of verifying analytical results produced by LLMs. The reliability of LLM-based features was assessed through a technical evaluation.

title: ImageDirector: Expressing Spatial Intent via 3D Direct Manipulation for Generative Image Editing
abstract: Generative image editing through text prompting suffers from two fundamental limitations: text is imprecise for specifying spatial changes, and iterative edits often introduce unwanted visual drift. In contrast, people naturally approach image editing with a compositor’s intuition: manipulating individual objects while expecting the rest of the scene to remain intact. We present ImageDirector, a generative image editing system that supports this intuition by enabling users to manipulate objects in a 2D generated image as if they exist in 3D space. Given a generated image, our system segments a selected object, turns it into a manipulable high-fidelity 3D proxy via image-to-3D lifting, and lets users reposition, rotate, and scale it through direct manipulation. The system then re-composites and harmonizes the result with background regions preserved. In a within-subjects study (N = 12), ImageDirector significantly outperformed a text-only prompting baseline in spatial accuracy and visual consistency across iterative edits; participants also reported substantially greater perceived control and expressiveness over the editing process. Finally, we discuss how this approach extends to broader content creation workflows, opening new possibilities for intuitive, precise, and controllable human-AI co-creation.

title: PersonaTeaming: Workflow and Interface that Support Persona-Driven Automated Generative AI Red-teaming
abstract: Recent developments in AI safety research have called for red-teaming methods—the practice of probing an AI system with adversarial inputs in order to surface harmful, biased, or otherwise problematic behaviors before deployment—that effectively surface potential risks posed by generative AI models, with growing emphasis on how red-teamers’ backgrounds and perspectives shape their strategies and the risks they uncover. While automated red-teaming approaches promise to complement human red-teaming through larger-scale exploration, existing automated approaches do not account for human identities and rarely incorporate human inputs. In this work, we explore persona-driven red-teaming to advance both automated red-teaming and human-AI collaboration. We first develop PersonaTeaming Workflow, which incorporates personas into the adversarial prompt generation process to explore a wider spectrum of adversarial strategies. Compared to RainbowPlus, a state-of-the-art automated red-teaming method, PersonaTeaming Workflow achieves higher attack success rates while maintaining prompt diversity. However, since automated personas only approximate real human perspectives, we further instantiate PersonaTeaming Workflow as PersonaTeaming Playground, a user-facing interface that enables red-teamers to author their own personas and collaborate with AI to mutate and refine prompts. In a user study with 11 industry practitioners, we found that PersonaTeaming Playground enabled diverse red-teaming strategies and outputs that practitioners perceived as useful, and that AI-generated suggestions in the PersonaTeaming Playground encouraged out-of-the-box thinking even when practitioners did not follow them strictly. Together, our work advances both automated and human-in-the-loop approaches to red-teaming, while shedding light on interaction patterns and design insights for supporting human-AI collaboration in generative AI red-teaming.

title: PATHWiSE: Empowering Teachers with a Generative AI Authoring System for Personalized Robot-Assisted Learning
abstract: Homework assignments often lack the personalized guidance and social interaction crucial for learning. Social robots offer a promising way to bring personalization and interactive support into learning activities; however, teachers rarely have the technical expertise needed to operate robots, let alone create or customize robot-assisted learning (RAL) lessons. To address this challenge, we introduce PATHWiSE, a robust, no-code authoring system designed to empower teachers to create custom RAL activities. Developed through participatory co-design activities with middle school science teachers and students and iteratively refined through multiple user studies, PATHWiSE enables educators to author, preview, and personalize RAL activities that can be tailored to different robot platforms and delivered with either in-person or on-screen robots. The system maintains a flexible trigger-action programming model to define robot expressions contextually related to lesson materials. Through integrated teacher- and student-facing portals, teachers can deploy RAL lessons using a lightweight and portable browser-based approach that affords integration with a wide range of systems. AI-assisted comment and emotion-expression generation tools augment teacher lesson creation while preserving teacher autonomy and expertise in content design. In this paper, we present the design and implementation of PATHWiSE, including its authoring workflow, interface architecture, backend integration, and representative use cases drawn from iterative studies to illustrate the capabilities of the full system.

title: BridgeScope: An Interactive System for Retrieving, Diagnosing, and Steering Cross-Modal SAE Features in Multimodal Large Models
abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have become a key tool for mechanistic interpretability via decomposing complex model representations into human-readable concepts. However, existing SAE analysis workflows focus mostly on language models. In multimodal settings, a major question remains: are SAE-based concepts shared across text and image modalities, or are they specific to each modality? In this paper, we present BridgeScope, an interactive system for retrieving, diagnosing, and validating cross-modal SAE features in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). BridgeScope integrates three capabilities: (1) input-driven feature retrieval that identifies features specifically activated by text, image, or joint input while filtering out globally frequent features; (2) multi-dimensional cross-modal diagnosis that evaluates features along cross-modal embedding similarity, modality balance, intra-modal coherence, and semantic similarity; and (3) steering-oriented intervention that enables users to manipulate features and examine both intended output changes and unintended side effects. Through quantitative evaluation, case studies, and a user study, we show that BridgeScope helps discover shared cross-modal features, diagnose their cross-modal properties, and support targeted interventions in MLLMs.

title: CoNarrate: Computationally Modeling Information Prematureness and Scaffolding the Co-Construction of Patient Narratives in Asynchronous Telehealth
abstract: Asynchronous telehealth requires patients to self-report their conditions, which serve as the critical basis for subsequent diagnosis and care. However, patients often struggle to articulate all necessary details upfront. This premature information delivery causes prolonged back-and-forth messaging, delayed clinical decisions, and increased physician burden. Comparing 5,000+ initial self-reports with post-consultation logs, we identified five recurring patterns of information prematureness. We model these patterns using the DIBH framework, mapping patient statements into a computable heterogeneous information space (Data, Information, Beliefs, Heuristics). Leveraging this underlying architecture, we developed CoNarrate, an LLM-driven intake system that proactively detects prematureness and generates targeted scaffolding questions before doctor review. A between-subjects study (N=46) demonstrated that CoNarrate significantly improved the clinical information richness of self-reports, reducing follow-up needs while maintaining high user satisfaction. This work contributes a new lens for modeling information prematureness, and a novel algorithmic approach to scaffolding the co-construction of comprehensive medical narratives.

title: Generating Personalized Games with Sensing Data to Support Self-Reported Data Collection
abstract: Collecting in-situ behavioral data to support research studies often involves prompting repeated ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) on smartphones and wearables. Sustained engagement, however, remains a major challenge because study participants often experience survey fatigue and declining motivation over time. To address this challenge, we introduce Personalized Adaptive Games for Engagement (PAGE): a novel LLM-powered approach that integrates data collection with a personalized game experience. PAGE uses a participant’s previously collected data to dynamically generate personalized puzzles, embedding behavioral data collection within engaging gameplay. We deployed a prototype using a variant of a word wheel puzzle game in a two-week feasibility study (N=15); while participants responded to EMAs in both weeks of the study, they also received sensor-based personalized puzzles in one of those weeks. We found that most participants (80%) preferred the week with personalized puzzles. Participants also contributed richer EMA data (72 additional unique contextual tags) and 1,188 additional uncompensated responses via a feasible in-game data collection channel during the puzzle week. We discuss design guidelines for developing context-aware personalized games to support engagement, potentially for use in longitudinal studies.

title: Exploring ChatGPT-Assisted Qualitative Data: Comparing Human and AI-Assisted Coding Using Braun and Clarke’s Thematic Analysis
abstract: The use of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models such as ChatGPT, has significantly expanded across academia and research in recent years. Of growing interest is AI’s potential role in qualitative research, especially in expediting tasks such as literature review and synthesis, data management and coding, and manuscript preparation, all while striving to maintain the rigor expected of qualitative inquiry. This paper explores the degree of alignment between AI-generated thematic analysis and a traditional, manual approach to analyzing focus group data and potential uses of AI in qualitative research. Using Braun and Clarke’s thematic analysis framework, a publicly available focus group dataset was analyzed in three stages: (1) Data Familiarization, (2) Human-Led Thematic Analysis, and (3) AI-Generated Analysis using ChatGPT. The human coders followed all six phases of the framework prior to engaging with the AI, to prevent influence from AI-generated output. The comparison revealed partial overlap between the human and AI-generated categories, particularly at the level of broader categories and themes. However, ChatGPT’s analysis tended to reflect a more superficial reading of the data, lacking the interpretive depth and nuance demonstrated by the human coders. While AI tools like ChatGPT show potential for supporting certain aspects of qualitative analysis, this study highlights key limitations in their ability to fully replicate the complexity and contextual understanding that human-led analysis provides. Further exploration is needed to define appropriate and ethical roles for AI in qualitative research workflows.

title: Codetations: Rich, Granular, and Maintainable Annotations for Evolving Code
abstract: Developers accumulate rich contextual knowledge about their code (e.g., design rationales, edge cases, worked examples) that does not fit in source files and goes stale when kept in separate documents or in human memory. We present Codetations, a VSCode extension enabling persistent, interactive annotations on arbitrary code spans without modifying the underlying file. A novel hybrid annotation anchoring method combines editor tracking for local edits with LLM-based semantic matching for offline changes, keeping annotations stable as code evolves. Annotation tools are modules sharing a minimal API for document access and state management. We demonstrate that this API is expressive enough to support multimedia embedding, automatic documentation maintenance, and external tool integration. In initial user studies with nine experienced developers, we found that attachment behavior matched their expectations. The diverse tools also enabled developers to imagine a variety of domain-specific use cases for annotations, particularly for validating and managing LLM-generated code. We discuss how a lightweight annotation layer can preserve contextual knowledge and open up a novel design space of developer-defined annotations.

title: PrejSense: Non-intrusive Gaze-Informed Prediction of Implicit Prejudice Against Machine for Proactive Interface Adaptation
abstract: Implicit prejudice against machine can critically undermine the effectiveness of human-AI collaboration by limiting trust, cooperation, and system acceptance. Despite its significance, such prejudice is rarely addressed in real world usage and is often assessed retrospectively through self-report measures or implicit association test, lacking automated and adaptive interface essential for responsive system design. Drawn from dual process theory, we propose and test PrejSense, a proof-of-concept adaptive interface loop that uses non-intrusive gaze signals to predict users’ prejudice states and adapt interface support accordingly. First, we develop interpretable deep learning models to predict prejudice from gaze features. Second, we develop adaptive interface using LLM agents to dynamically respond to estimated prejudice states, with expert-informed refinement. Third, we build a full-stack system for automated prejudice prediction and adaptive interaction, enabling non-intrusive integration into collaborative AI systems. We conduct a user testing experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of PrejSense. Compared with baseline, PrejSense significantly enhanced emotional trust and showed marginal positive effects on cognitive trust and WOA. These results provide preliminary evidence for state-contingent prejudice-aware adaptation in a low-risk decision-support task. By combining gaze-informed prejudice prediction with adaptive interaction design, this work opens a design space for prejudice-aware adaptive interfaces while highlighting the need for larger-scale validation.

title: MoTUI: Personalization of In-Vehicle Tactile Interfaces for People With Vision Impairments and the Blind
abstract: Configuring in-vehicle interfaces for people with vision impairments (VIPs) requires jointly tuning buttons, feedback modalities, layout, and speech parameters. This defines a design space too large for manual exploration, with inherently conflicting objectives such as maximizing situation awareness while minimizing cognitive load. Prior work recognizes personalization as critical but offers no systematic method to achieve it. We contribute MoTUI, an open-source Modular Tactile User Interface with reconfigurable hardware and software for runtime exploration of this design space and replication of existing designs. MoTUI is configuration-agnostic and supports multiple personalization strategies; we instantiate and evaluate one, pairing it with Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization (HITL-MOBO) to navigate the space efficiently. In a within-subject study (N = 12 VIPs), HITL-optimized configurations outperformed a static baseline and an LLM-generated design on situation awareness, perceived workload, and satisfaction, with significant gains over the LLM-based approach. For psychological ownership, optimized configurations were rated significantly higher than both baselines. Importantly, optimization converged on substantially different configurations across participants, indicating strong individual differences; qualitative findings further explain these personalized outcomes.

title: MemCanvas: A Structured Memory Canvas for Evolving Intent Alignment in LLM Dialogues
abstract: Aligning user intent in complex, evolving dialogues with Large Language Models (LLMs) is a significant challenge. We attribute this to a cognitive divergence between LLM’s linear reasoning based on context and statistical semantic representations, and the exploratory, non-linear, and personalized nature of human intent. These gaps not only cause progressive misalignment but also leave users without a clear understanding of model’s perception or means to control its trajectory. To bridge this gap, we introduce MemCanvas, an interactive system that organizes dialogue history into shared, editable memory structures to complement outcome-based approaches. By scaffolding intent via three interaction primitives—Trees (for thematic directions), Relations (for logical connections), and Tags (for personalized semantics)—MemCanvas enables users to externalize evolving intent and proactively steer the LLM’s reasoning. Our technical evaluation and user study (N=28) demonstrate that MemCanvas effectively aligns user intent and enhances users’ sense of control, transparency and collaboration. Ultimately, this work illustrates how intent scaffolding can serve as a practical supplement to standard linear interfaces, fostering more process-aligned human-AI collaboration.

title: KnowTap: A Knowledge-Driven Tool for Fine-Grained Tappability Assessment and Design Iteration of Mobile UIs
abstract: Visually perceived tappability, defined as the degree to which a static UI component looks interactive, is critical to interface usability and distinct from physical target acquisition, yet existing task-specific models generally provide binary labels. However, designers need finer-grained tappability assessments to make informed modifications during iterative design. To address this, we propose KnowTap, a Figma-compatible interactive tool that predicts continuous perceived-tappability scores from mean human ratings collected on a 0–5 annotation scale, visualizes them in six display bands, and provides optional LLM-generated feedback to suggest context-aware improvements. Using a new dataset of 800 mobile UIs and 9,751 components whose GPT-4o pre-labels were corrected by three independent crowdworker groups, KnowTap combines structured design knowledge, text-derived features, and deep embeddings in a random forest regressor that achieves SRCC.745 and R2.564 under UI-grouped five-fold cross-validation, compared with.646 and.387 for an adapted, randomly initialized Taperception-style ResNet-18 baseline, while offering attribute-level explanations complementary to prior pixel-level saliency. In a within-subjects study with 12 designers, paired comparisons showed higher reported satisfaction and perceived task success and lower mental demand, temporal demand, and frustration in the six-band condition, and independent raters preferred its resulting designs in three of four test UIs. Our research contributes a knowledge-driven tool for continuous perceived-tappability prediction, along with a new dataset, to support Figma-compatible mobile-UI design iteration.

title: Precise Duration Control for Video Editing via LLM Scoring and Constrained Optimization
abstract: Editing videos calls for satisfying two fundamentally different kinds of requirements simultaneously. Editors often need to meet hard constraints, such as hitting a precise target duration, while also considering semantic objectives, such as preferring engaging content. These two requirements lend themselves to different computational tools, and combining them is non-trivial. Using video editing as a case study, we present a hybrid approach that combines using LLMs to provide semantically relevant labels for video clips with using mixed-integer linear programming to enforce hard constraints and select content. Our approach guarantees millisecond-precise output durations while optimizing for user-specified semantic objectives, such as informativity and topic relevance. Feedback from editors indicates that our tool supports interactive exploration across several video editing goals, including creating interview rough cuts and shortening edited videos for sharing across different platforms.

title: Less Is More: Balancing Positive and Negative Space in Visual Concept Blending
abstract: Graphic designers often blend visual concepts to communicate multiple ideas within a single image, leveraging positive and negative space to create balance, emphasis, and aesthetic appeal. While computational methods have begun to support automatic concept blending, they largely overlook the role of spatial composition in the design. To address this gap, we present an automatic pipeline that explicitly applies positive and negative space throughout the blending process. Our approach first identifies plausible regions for concept integration by combining semantic reasoning from vision–language models with geometric constraints derived from real-world examples. Conditioned on these regions, the system generates blended compositions using a hybrid pixel–vector pipeline: diffusion-based inpainting produces a fast, coarse initialization, which is then refined through vector-based optimization at the point level to ensure structural coherence and balanced semantic expression. A multimodal agent orchestrates this process as a planner and evaluator, enabling iterative improvement and interpretable control. Through an evaluation using both baseline comparisons and a user study, we demonstrate greater expressiveness, creativity, and concept recognizability by effectively leveraging positive and negative space. We further demonstrate the generalizability of our approach across diverse applications, including controllable image and infographic generation.

title: Prism-UX: Turning Evaluative Divergence into Traceable Design Evidence for LLM-Based Process-Level UX Evaluation
abstract: Generative AI is increasingly being integrated into interactive workflows, introducing new challenges for UX evaluation because user experience is becoming more context-dependent and more closely tied to process-level moments such as waiting, flicker, uncertainty, intermediate artifacts, and loss of control. However, existing AI-assisted evaluation methods often compress such process-level differences into a single decontextualized conclusion. Interviews with 10 practitioners revealed that reviewers often struggle to cite specific moments in an interaction, compare interpretations across stakeholders, or trace their judgments back to observable facts. We refer to this loss of perspective-specific evaluative distinctions as insight collapse. To address this problem, we propose Prism-UX, a traceable review system for short, visually observable UI workflows involving GenAI features. Prism-UX first transforms interaction screen recordings into citable storyboard evidence through a frame-difference algorithm, then supports side-by-side evaluation from configurable evaluative viewpoints over shared evidence, and finally applies a structured reasoning protocol that anchors review judgments in explicit Fact IDs. Through a technical ablation study and expert evaluation, Prism-UX reduced the logical conflict rate by 84%, increased grounding completeness from 0.38 to 0.82, and was rated more useful than automated baselines for trade-off inspection, discussion support, and decision confidence. The results suggest that preserving evidence-grounded evaluative disagreement, rather than forcing convergence, can support more traceable and disagreement-aware design review.

title: Understanding the Role of AI-Enabled Live Tables in Scholarly Sensemaking
abstract: AI-assisted tools are increasingly used to support information extraction and multi-document reading in research workflows. However, conventional conversational LLM interfaces often mismatch researchers’ specific needs, potentially inducing unnecessary cognitive load. To explore more effective interaction paradigms, we developed Lignin, an academic literature reading tool centered on tabular information representation and real-time AI querying. Building on existing table-based reading tools, Lignin combines dynamically configurable query columns, per-cell regeneration and editing, and source-level traceability. This design allows users to revise query dimensions as their questions evolve and supports cross-document comparison during scholarly sensemaking. A controlled experiment was conducted to examine the impact of this tool versus traditional AI interaction modes on cognitive activities during exploratory tasks in unfamiliar domains. Through observations and interviews, we identified instances in which participants appeared to benefit from particular design features, clarifying how different information formats and interaction styles influence such tasks. These findings offer valuable insights for the design of future AI-assisted reading tools and the optimization of AI-mediated research practices.
